articles.title: Hundreds of thousands still without power after storms hit US on Thanksgiving
articles.summary: Pennsylvania and neighbouring states remain badly affected on Friday after both coasts were lashed with wind and rain.
articles.content:
Watch: Roofs torn off and streets under water as severe weather hits the US

Hundreds of thousands of people are without power after severe weather hit both coasts of the United States during the Thanksgiving holiday.

Eastern areas were lashed on Thursday by a powerful storm which brought high winds, heavy rain and coastal flooding. Pennsylvania remained the state worst hit by power cuts early on Friday, according to monitoring site Poweroutage.us.

Conditions are now expected to improve, though forecasters caution that it will take some time. The West Coast has also been affected by its own storms.

Flight disruption also persists, with hundreds more delays and cancellations reported on Friday - which is expected to be another busy travel day.

More than 2,500 flights within, into or out of the US were delayed on Thursday, and more than 450 were cancelled, according to Flightaware.com.

One passenger told the BBC he had been stuck at New York's LaGuardia Airport for 13 hours while trying to fly to see friends in Chicago for Thanksgiving.

Beyond the travel disruption, impacts were widespread across the East Coast, and US President Donald Trump said he would consider releasing emergency funds.

Bridges closed in Maryland due to severe winds, while waves battered beaches in Delaware as water seeped onto the boardwalk.

On the wettest Thanksgiving on record in Washington DC, tidal waters surged and soaked runways at Reagan Washington National Airport.

Parts of some states are under states of emergency, including New York.

Nearly 2in (5cm) of rain fell on New York City's iconic Central Park, making it the wettest Thanksgiving on record at that site as well, according to preliminary data , external from the NWS.

Organisers of the city's annual Macy's Thanksgiving parade have also pushed back the event to Saturday - marking the event's first postponement in its 100-year history.

In neighbouring New Jersey, there were multiple reports of closed roads and bridges, and images of floodwater blanketing city streets.

"This is wild," an Ocean City, New Jersey-based blogger said in a video , external posted on social media, as he waded through water splashing above his waist.

The number of homes reporting power cuts peaked at close to a million on Thursday evening - with Pennsylvania, Virginia, Maryland and New Jersey badly affected.

Pennsylvania Governor Josh Shapiro said utility providers were working tirelessly to restore power. In Maryland, almost two million customers were asked by authorities to limit their water consumption to essential use only due to "intermittent power disruptions".

The storm is expected to ease on Friday and move into the Canadian provinces of Nova Scotia and Newfoundland on Saturday, leaving a much drier weekend for the north-eastern United States, according to the Met Office.

However, another deep area of low pressure will likely arrive on Monday - bringing another spell of heavy rain and strong winds, and some further travel disruption.

The particularly high tide in California caused huge waves to crash over the wall in Pacifica, where a portion of the municipal pier collapsed

On the West Coast, the concern was for exceptionally high tides and the associated risk of flooding.

Both San Diego and Los Angeles reported a high tide of over 8ft (2.4m) earlier this week, and beach-goers were advised to avoid coastal areas.

Train services along the Amtrak Pacific Surfliner, which runs along the California coastline, cancelled several trains due to "washout conditions from high tides", the company shared on social media.

Dramatic footage from Oregon showed a man and a dog being swept into the sea by a fierce, so-called king tide - but both escaped unharmed, police said.

In Miami, some travel delays persisted into Thursday after a FedEx plane overshot the runway the night before, which prompted the closure of all but one runway at the airport for a brief period.

A statement FedEx provided to US media confirmed that one of its flights had "experienced an issue upon landing". No injuries were reported, and the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) is investigating what happened.

An airport employee who spoke anonymously to CBS News, the BBC's US partner, raised the possibility that rainy conditions had been a factor.

The American Automobile Association (AAA) predicted that 81.5 million Americans will travel at least 50 miles (80km) from home for the Thanksgiving holiday over a seven-day period.

Massive waves crashed into the Pacifica Pier in Pacifica, California on Wednesday

articles.title: Tyson Fury cleared to fight Anthony Joshua after mental health concerns allayed
articles.summary: British Boxing Board of Control will license fight Claim of Fury’s schizophrenia diagnosis was retracted Tyson Fury has been cleared to fight Anthony Joshua in Cardiff next month despite concerns about his mental health. The British Boxing Board of ­Control (BBBoC) indicated this week that it would investigate comments from Fury’s wife, Paris, that the boxer had been diagnosed with ­schizophrenia, and had the powers to deny him a licence to fight. Continue reading...
articles.content:
Tyson Fury has been cleared to fight Anthony Joshua in Cardiff next month despite concerns about his mental health.

The British Boxing Board of ­Control (BBBofC) indicated this week that it would investigate comments from Fury’s wife, Paris, that the boxer had been diagnosed with ­schizophrenia, and had the powers to deny him a licence to fight.

Paris Fury retracted her claim in a statement issued on Thursday night, and the BBBofC’s general secretary Robert Smith told Sky Sports: “Fury cleared last night. All up to date medicals cleared. Promoter told this morning.”

Paris Fury had said in an initial ­version of a Netflix documentary released on Friday that Fury was diagnosed with schizophrenia just months after beating Wladimir Klitschko to win the world heavyweight title in Düsseldorf in November 2015.

She said in Thursday’s statement: “I want to clarify a statement I made in the original version of the Tyson Fury documentary.

“I recalled a conversation from many years ago when discussing Tyson’s condition and I used the word ‘schizophrenic’. Whilst Tyson did show some symptoms associated with schizophrenia, he doesn’t have this condition and has never received a diagnosis.

“Mental health is complex, and it isn’t always easy to find the right words, especially when you’re living it with someone you love. I’m so proud of Tyson for really opening up in this documentary and want to say thank you for all the support we’ve received as a family.”

Netflix indicated it had edited the footage as a result, saying in a statement: “Following new information shared by the family relating to Tyson’s official mental health diagnosis, we have worked alongside them to update the documentary accordingly ahead of launch.”

Fury himself had also told the Guardian last week that he had been diagnosed with the condition, saying: “I went to a ­leading specialist and was diagnosed with schizophrenia and bipolar. I learned that you can never truly get away from mental health. You can only learn to manage and maintain.”

He has been open about his mental health struggles since beating Klitschko, after which he took a near three-year hiatus from boxing, with his weight ballooning to 27 stone, while he contended with suicidal thoughts and alcohol addiction.

Fury admitted hearing “voices in my mind” following his win, adding: “Words can’t explain the darkness I was in.

“I came from the living version of the pits of hellfire. And I 100% thought at times I’d end up in a padded room with the door locked, and that scared me so much.”

The Fury v Joshua bout is set to take place at Cardiff’s ­Principality Stadium in the early hours of 12 December in UK time, with the undercard ­beginning in the evening of the 11th.

articles.title: Anh Do: ‘When your mum believes in you, you’ve got no option but to make sure you succeed’
articles.summary: The standup comedian, writer and artist on what made him stop doing art, and the tragedy that prompted him to pick up a paintbrush again Sign up for a weekly email featuring our best reads Most Tafe students are fresh out of high school. articles.content:
The standup comedian, writer and artist on what made him stop doing art, and the tragedy that prompted him to pick up a paintbrush again

Most Tafe students are fresh out of high school. So when a 35-year-old Anh Do walked in one day to begin a fine art course – already a successful comedian and author – it turned some heads.

“This 18-year-old bloke comes up to me and goes, ‘Geez, you look like Anh Do.’ I said, ‘Yeah, that’s because I am.’ And he goes, ‘Nah, you’re not, but you bloody look like him,’ and walks off,” Do says. He eventually convinced the teenager that he was, in fact, the real Anh Do – and a friendship was born. “I’m still mates with him now!”

I believe him – within a few minutes of meeting Do, now 49, it’s clear he is one of those people with the preternatural ability to befriend anyone. Standing at our meeting spot outside a large converted warehouse in the Sydney suburb of Newtown, Do spots me first – he cartoonishly swivels around, erupts with an oversized wave and tells me how excited he is for our chat. He then launches into jovial, mile-a-minute conversation before I can even clip his mic on. Do is full of anecdotes like his Tafe run-in – some of which are written on the palm of his hand, so he doesn’t forget to bring them up (“I’m just going to give you my best stories, and you put in whatever you want to!”).

As one of the country’s best-loved comedians, Do knows a bit about collecting funny stories. Before his stint as the most famous mature-aged student at Tafe, Do was a standup comic who delivered punchlines about life as the only Vietnamese kid at Yagoona high and what he’d call his anti-Pauline Hanson political party (“One Asian”). He quickly picked up roles on shows such as SeaChange and Pizza, and then came his bestselling memoir, The Happiest Refugee, which charted how his family arrived in Australia on an overcrowded fishing boat in 1980, battling starvation and two different sets of pirates along the way (“With stories like that, I just had to not botch it!”). From there, Do pivoted to becoming a children’s author (he has now published 120 kids’ books, which he writes from his hotel rooms while on tour), and host of a hit TV show (we’ll get to that.)

Do’s passion for painting and drawing started early, here in Newtown. I knew Do had asked to meet here, in this exact spot, to show me one of his former childhood homes. I didn’t realise we were already standing right next to it.

“We freakin’ lived in that!” he says, gesturing up at the impressive building to our left.

The building we are looking up at is now a large luxury home last purchased by a former casino boss in 2023 for $13.5m. But in the 1980s, it was a warehouse that Do’s extended family moved into alongside two other tenants; his mum and aunties working overtime to meet seamstressing deadlines in one corner of the room while the kids tried to sleep in the other. Do moved between 20 different homes throughout his childhood but this one has a special spot in his heart – it’s the place where he realised how much joy art could bring himself and others.

At dinnertime, eight-year-old Do would sit and sketch his uncles and cousins. When everyone had finished eating, his dad would shush the family and instruct Do to reveal what he’d drawn.

“I’d spin the finished drawing around and everyone would cheer, ‘Yeah, it looks just like him!’ Or, ‘No, you’ve made him too handsome!’” Do grins. “But it used to make everyone so happy.”

Years later, that very same format would be mirrored in the hit ABC TV show Anh’s Brush with Fame, although that set-up required him to paint while steering a poignant conversation with a string of prominent Australians before revealing their portrait to them.

This neighbourhood – now home to many a $40 share plate – is, Do admits, “very different” to what it was in his day but he displays no cynicism about the gentrification. Do really seems to be the affable guy his memoir title sold him as. Never more than a minute or two passes in our conversation without laughter, his everyman Aussie charm (Do will say “mate” 17 times in our 45-minute conversation) and enthusiasm radiating all the while. (“So we just walk around? What a great idea!” he says, getting his head around today’s interview format.)

The good times in Newtown wouldn’t last for Do’s family. He would only live in the warehouse for two years, with money becoming tight and the family’s living situation more tenuous after his dad abruptly left the family when Do was 13. Do now knows his father was grappling with untreated PTSD from the Vietnam War but at the time his departure was a blow.

“I couldn’t understand that this guy who was such an awesome dad would just disappear,” Do says as we start slowly strolling through Camperdown Park, passing tattooed young people sunbathing on the grass. It changed him: “I stopped [painting] when Dad left and that little voice of encouragement disappeared”.

Do put down the paint brush and fixated on the idea of becoming a lawyer – determined to secure a high-paying career so he could buy his mum a house. He was nearing university graduation with multiple job offers to choose from when he had a last-minute change of heart.

“I discovered that these guys work 60-plus hours a week,” Do says. “At the same time, I’ve got a comedian friend, Dave [Grant]. I said, ‘Daveo, how many hours a week do you work?’ And he goes, ‘about four’.” Grant told his friend how much he made and “it wasn’t far off the first-year law graduate salary … I’m going to switch!” he says, the laughter returning. Do’s mother gave her blessing, “and when your mum believes in you that much, you’ve got no option but to make sure you succeed”.

When Do eventually tracked down and reconnected with his father in his early 20s, one of the first questions his dad asked was if his son was still painting.

“I said, ‘a little bit’, but I was lying,” Do says as he steers us away from a small cemetery (“I’ll feel like I have to stop talking if we walk down there”) and on to a shady residential street. “[Dad] was like, ‘mate, you’ve got to get back into that’.”

But with his comedy and writing career firing, it would take more than a decade for Do to heed his father’s advice. It wasn’t until the friend who’d encouraged him into comedy – Dave Grant – died from pancreatic cancer that Do stopped telling himself he’d get around to painting again when he retired.

“It shocked me and broke my heart, and I thought to myself, ‘Well, what if I don’t get to 70?’” he says with a matter-of-fact shrug. “That’s when I booked into Tafe.”

A teacher – “and he became a good mate as well” – told Do that he would have to do a hundred paintings before he “got good”, so he spent the next two years devotedly putting paint to canvas on 200 different creations.

“And he’s right. I did get good, because I made the Archibald in 2014,” Do grins.

That would become one of five times Do has now reached the finals; in 2017 he even nabbed the Archibald people’s choice prize with his portrait of Indigenous actor and activist Jack Charles. Do is modest about that success – the beauty of Australia’s biggest art prize, he says, is that anyone can submit their work.

Do’s Archibald paintings will be among the works on display at his first ever art exhibition, opening 28 November at Newcastle Art Gallery. His dad – with whom Do repaired his relationship, and who he says is now “my best mate” – will be there. Given how long it took him to pursue art professionally, snagging his debut exhibition at nearly 50 feels like a big deal. But Do has no plans to stop doing comedy or writing (“Standup is at night, so I’ve got all day to kill time”).

We’ve slowly ambled our way around the park and surrounding streets, looping back to our meeting place, outside the now palatial home where Do spent so many evenings sketching. There’s time to wedge in one last question before we have to part ways: with so much to his CV, what does Do feel he still has left to achieve?

“I used to think like that, but I don’t any more,” he says after a long pause – lost for words for the first time today. “If I just get to do what I’m doing now until I die – hopefully, fingers crossed, at a nice old age – I’ll be very content.”
paragraphs: The standup comedian, writer and artist on what made him stop doing art, and the tragedy that prompted him to pick up a paintbrush again
Most Tafe students are fresh out of high school. So when a 35-year-old Anh Do walked in one day to begin a fine art course – already a successful comedian and author – it turned some heads.

“This 18-year-old bloke comes up to me and goes, ‘Geez, you look like Anh Do.’ I said, ‘Yeah, that’s because I am.’ And he goes, ‘Nah, you’re not, but you bloody look like him,’ and walks off,” Do says. He eventually convinced the teenager that he was, in fact, the real Anh Do – and a friendship was born. “I’m still mates with him now!”

I believe him – within a few minutes of meeting Do, now 49, it’s clear he is one of those people with the preternatural ability to befriend anyone. Standing at our meeting spot outside a large converted warehouse in the Sydney suburb of Newtown, Do spots me first – he cartoonishly swivels around, erupts with an oversized wave and tells me how excited he is for our chat. He then launches into jovial, mile-a-minute conversation before I can even clip his mic on. Do is full of anecdotes like his Tafe run-in – some of which are written on the palm of his hand, so he doesn’t forget to bring them up (“I’m just going to give you my best stories, and you put in whatever you want to!”).

As one of the country’s best-loved comedians, Do knows a bit about collecting funny stories. Before his stint as the most famous mature-aged student at Tafe, Do was a standup comic who delivered punchlines about life as the only Vietnamese kid at Yagoona high and what he’d call his anti-Pauline Hanson political party (“One Asian”). He quickly picked up roles on shows such as SeaChange and Pizza, and then came his bestselling memoir, The Happiest Refugee, which charted how his family arrived in Australia on an overcrowded fishing boat in 1980, battling starvation and two different sets of pirates along the way (“With stories like that, I just had to not botch it!”). From there, Do pivoted to becoming a children’s author (he has now published 120 kids’ books, which he writes from his hotel rooms while on tour), and host of a hit TV show (we’ll get to that.)

Do’s passion for painting and drawing started early, here in Newtown. I knew Do had asked to meet here, in this exact spot, to show me one of his former childhood homes. I didn’t realise we were already standing right next to it.
“We freakin’ lived in that!” he says, gesturing up at the impressive building to our left.

The building we are looking up at is now a large luxury home last purchased by a former casino boss in 2023 for $13.5m. But in the 1980s, it was a warehouse that Do’s extended family moved into alongside two other tenants; his mum and aunties working overtime to meet seamstressing deadlines in one corner of the room while the kids tried to sleep in the other. Do moved between 20 different homes throughout his childhood but this one has a special spot in his heart – it’s the place where he realised how much joy art could bring himself and others.
At dinnertime, eight-year-old Do would sit and sketch his uncles and cousins. When everyone had finished eating, his dad would shush the family and instruct Do to reveal what he’d drawn.
“I’d spin the finished drawing around and everyone would cheer, ‘Yeah, it looks just like him!’ Or, ‘No, you’ve made him too handsome!’” Do grins. “But it used to make everyone so happy.”

Years later, that very same format would be mirrored in the hit ABC TV show Anh’s Brush with Fame, although that set-up required him to paint while steering a poignant conversation with a string of prominent Australians before revealing their portrait to them.

This neighbourhood – now home to many a $40 share plate – is, Do admits, “very different” to what it was in his day but he displays no cynicism about the gentrification. Do really seems to be the affable guy his memoir title sold him as. Never more than a minute or two passes in our conversation without laughter, his everyman Aussie charm (Do will say “mate” 17 times in our 45-minute conversation) and enthusiasm radiating all the while. (“So we just walk around? What a great idea!” he says, getting his head around today’s interview format.)

The good times in Newtown wouldn’t last for Do’s family. He would only live in the warehouse for two years, with money becoming tight and the family’s living situation more tenuous after his dad abruptly left the family when Do was 13. Do now knows his father was grappling with untreated PTSD from the Vietnam War but at the time his departure was a blow.

“I couldn’t understand that this guy who was such an awesome dad would just disappear,” Do says as we start slowly strolling through Camperdown Park, passing tattooed young people sunbathing on the grass. It changed him: “I stopped [painting] when Dad left and that little voice of encouragement disappeared”.

Do put down the paint brush and fixated on the idea of becoming a lawyer – determined to secure a high-paying career so he could buy his mum a house. He was nearing university graduation with multiple job offers to choose from when he had a last-minute change of heart.

“I discovered that these guys work 60-plus hours a week,” Do says. “At the same time, I’ve got a comedian friend, Dave [Grant]. I said, ‘Daveo, how many hours a week do you work?’ And he goes, ‘about four’.” Grant told his friend how much he made and “it wasn’t far off the first-year law graduate salary … I’m going to switch!” he says, the laughter returning. Do’s mother gave her blessing, “and when your mum believes in you that much, you’ve got no option but to make sure you succeed”.
When Do eventually tracked down and reconnected with his father in his early 20s, one of the first questions his dad asked was if his son was still painting.

“I said, ‘a little bit’, but I was lying,” Do says as he steers us away from a small cemetery (“I’ll feel like I have to stop talking if we walk down there”) and on to a shady residential street. “[Dad] was like, ‘mate, you’ve got to get back into that’.”

But with his comedy and writing career firing, it would take more than a decade for Do to heed his father’s advice. It wasn’t until the friend who’d encouraged him into comedy – Dave Grant – died from pancreatic cancer that Do stopped telling himself he’d get around to painting again when he retired.
“It shocked me and broke my heart, and I thought to myself, ‘Well, what if I don’t get to 70?’” he says with a matter-of-fact shrug. “That’s when I booked into Tafe.”

A teacher – “and he became a good mate as well” – told Do that he would have to do a hundred paintings before he “got good”, so he spent the next two years devotedly putting paint to canvas on 200 different creations.
“And he’s right. I did get good, because I made the Archibald in 2014,” Do grins.

That would become one of five times Do has now reached the finals; in 2017 he even nabbed the Archibald people’s choice prize with his portrait of Indigenous actor and activist Jack Charles. Do is modest about that success – the beauty of Australia’s biggest art prize, he says, is that anyone can submit their work.

Do’s Archibald paintings will be among the works on display at his first ever art exhibition, opening 28 November at Newcastle Art Gallery. His dad – with whom Do repaired his relationship, and who he says is now “my best mate” – will be there. Given how long it took him to pursue art professionally, snagging his debut exhibition at nearly 50 feels like a big deal. But Do has no plans to stop doing comedy or writing (“Standup is at night, so I’ve got all day to kill time”).

We’ve slowly ambled our way around the park and surrounding streets, looping back to our meeting place, outside the now palatial home where Do spent so many evenings sketching. There’s time to wedge in one last question before we have to part ways: with so much to his CV, what does Do feel he still has left to achieve?

“I used to think like that, but I don’t any more,” he says after a long pause – lost for words for the first time today. “If I just get to do what I’m doing now until I die – hopefully, fingers crossed, at a nice old age – I’ll be very content.”

articles.title: French and Bulgarian presidents condemn violence at Marseille v Levski Europa League game
articles.summary: Emmanuel Macron: incidents had ‘no place in sport’ Nazi salutes alleged among Levski Sofia fans The presidents of France and Bulgaria have condemned violence that broke out at a Europa League fixture between Marseille and Levski Sofia in the Stade Vélodrome. Television footage showed Marseille fans cornering a group of Levski supporters in the stands before beating them relentlessly, including with a belt. One Levski fan is seen bleeding from the head as he receives multiple blows while trying to protect a female friend. Reports from inside the stadium on Thursday suggested violence began after a Levski supporter was seen making a Nazi salute. Continue reading...
articles.content:
The presidents of France and Bulgaria have condemned violence that broke out at a Europa League fixture between Marseille and Levski Sofia in the Stade Vélodrome.

Television footage showed Marseille fans cornering a group of Levski supporters in the stands before beating them relentlessly, including with a belt. One Levski fan is seen bleeding from the head as he receives multiple blows while trying to protect a female friend. Reports from inside the stadium on Thursday suggested violence began after a Levski supporter was seen making a Nazi salute.

The Marseille prosecutor’s office said it would open an investigation into the trouble, specifically accusations that French fans committed “aggravated intentional violence” against Levski supporters, and that it would also pursue allegations of “incitement to hatred after Nazi salutes and provocations from the Bulgarian fans”.

A statement on behalf of the French president, Emmanuel Macron, on Friday said he condemned the violence “in the strongest possible terms” and that it had “no place in sport or in public places”. He also insisted “these acts would not go unpunished”.

The Bulgarian president, Iliana Iotova, described the violence as “unacceptable” and “shocking” and said: “The attacks against the Bulgarian fans desecrate one of the great games that brings millions of people together around the world. Everyone should be able to support their team without being afraid for their safety.”

The country’s prime minister, Rumen Radev, said he had spoken to Macron about the incident which had resulted in 11 Bulgarian fans being hurt, five of whom were taken to hospital.

“We share the position that aggression and violence have no place in civilised Europe,” Radev said. “I thank President Macron for his personal commitment to this case, for the medical care provided to the injured by the French authorities, for the measures taken to ensure the safety of Bulgarian citizens, and for the perpetrators to be held accountable.”

Another Europa League fixture on Thursday, between Besiktas and Hapoel Beer Sheva, was suspended for 30 minutes owing to fighting. Uefa’s account of the disruption that occurred at a neutral venue in Batumi, Georgia, said the game had been suspended to allow local police to subdue fighting between Besiktas supporters. Besiktas condemned what it called “disproportionate force” by security staff and said some fans had been denied entry.

Turkey’s football federation strongly condemned what it described as “unacceptable” actions undertaken by Georgian police targeting Besiktas supporters who unfurled a pro-Palestine banner during the match.

A Uefa statement, however, said: “Uefa understands that the escalation between the local police and Besiktas’ supporters – which caused the temporary suspension of the match – started following an intervention of the local police in the sector of the Besiktas supporters to neutralise clashes that had erupted amongst Besiktas’ own supporters.”

Uefa condemned the violence at both matches and said it had appointed inspectors to conduct disciplinary investigations. “Uefa competitions are founded on the principles of respect, fair play, integrity and safety,” a statement said. “The events witnessed at the above-mentioned matches run counter to these fundamental values.” Any investigation would “examine all available evidence to establish the relevant facts and circumstances”, the statement said.

Last season Marseille were hit with a partial stadium closure after fans launched fireworks and pointed lasers into the field during a Champions League fixture against Atalanta.

articles.title: Cocktail of the week: A Bar with Shapes for a Name’s honey-washed bourbon boulevardier – recipe | The good mixer
articles.summary: Courtesy of A Bar with Shapes for a Name in east London, this butter-infused variation on the classic is the perfect make-ahead drink for the festive season This twist on the classic drink uses honey-butter bourbon made with a simple fat-washing technique. It’s a brilliant standby for the festive season, not least because, save for the final mix, all the work is done in advance. Paul Lougrat, co-founder, A Bar with Shapes for a Name , London E2 Continue reading...
articles.content:
Courtesy of A Bar with Shapes for a Name in east London, this butter-infused variation on the classic is the perfect make-ahead drink for the festive season

T his twist on the classic drink uses honey-butter bourbon made with a simple fat-washing technique. It’s a brilliant standby for the festive season, not least because, save for the final mix, all the work is done in advance.

For the honey-butter bourbon (makes enough to serve 9) 60g unsalted butter 60g blossom honey 300ml bourbon – we use Buffalo Trace

For the drink 40ml honey-butter bourbon (see above and method) 20ml sweet red vermouth – we use Martini Rosso 17½ml Campari 1 dash salt solution – simply combine one part table salt with four parts filtered water and stir to dissolve; once made, it will keep in the fridge almost indefinitely 1 strip orange peel , to finish

First make the honey-butter bourbon. In a small saucepan, gently melt the butter and honey, stirring until fully combined. Stir in the bourbon, then take off the heat and leave to infuse at room temperature for an hour. Once cool, pour the mix into a clean, freezer-proof container, then put in the freezer until the butter has completely solidified – ideally, leave it overnight. Fine-strain the bourbon through a coffee filter into a clean jar or bottle, and discard the solidified butter. Seal and keep in the fridge for up to three months.

To build the drink, measure the bourbon, vermouth and Campari into a mixing glass filled with ice, add a dash of salt solution and stir until thoroughly chilled. Strain into a chilled coupe, squeeze the orange peel over the surface of the drink to release its oils, then drop it into the glass and serve immediately.

articles.summary: Don’t settle for another turkey sandwich. Here are eight exciting ways to reinvent Thanksgiving leftovers Download Feast , with more than 8,000 global recipes from Guardian chefs like Yotam Ottolenghi and Meera Sodha There’s only so much turkey sandwich a person can eat. Luckily, Thanksgiving leftovers are a delicious excuse to make something entirely new. From crispy hoisin pancakes to a fragrant turkey pho to a golden, cheesy gratin, here are eight ways to give yesterday’s bird a second life – or explore more recipes in our huge collection . Continue reading...
articles.content:
Don’t settle for another turkey sandwich. Here are eight exciting ways to reinvent Thanksgiving leftovers

Download Feast , with more than 8,000 global recipes from Guardian chefs like Yotam Ottolenghi and Meera Sodha

T here’s only so much turkey sandwich a person can eat. Luckily, Thanksgiving leftovers are a delicious excuse to make something entirely new. From crispy hoisin pancakes to a fragrant turkey pho to a golden, cheesy gratin, here are eight ways to give yesterday’s bird a second life – or explore more recipes in our huge collection .

With a few vegetables and hours of gentle simmering, a turkey carcass becomes a golden stock for soups, pastas and anything you’re cooking in the weeks ahead.

1 cooked turkey carcass , with remaining skin and meat attached, stuffing removed 1 carrot 1 onion 1 celery stalk 2 bay leaves

Weigh the turkey carcass then put it in a large stockpot with the veg and bay leaves. Add about 2½ quarts of water for every pound of meat and bones. Put it on the lowest possible heat for a couple of hours. You’ll be left with a lovely stock for risotto, soups, or to freeze to use later.

Turkey meat is perfect for curries, and this recipe uses curry paste and quick-cook veg, so it takes no time at all to prepare and serve. Serve with a steaming mound of basmati rice.

2–2¼ lb skinless cooked turkey meat 1 lb zucchini 9 oz grape or cherry tomatoes 2 tbsp butter 2 tbsp canola oil 3-5 tsp tikka curry paste or mild curry paste 1 (13.5-oz) can coconut milk A handful of fresh cilantro leaves

Cut the cooked turkey meat into smallish pieces. Trim the ends of the zucchini and slice across fairly thinly. Halve the tomatoes lengthwise.

Heat the butter and oil in a large, deep pan over medium-high heat. When the butter has melted, add the zucchini and tomatoes and stir for 2–3 minutes, until the zucchini begins to soften but hasn’t lost its bite.

Next, add the curry paste and the sliced turkey. Stir over the heat for another minute or so.

Lastly, pour in the coconut milk, stir and bring just up to bubbling. Remove from the heat, add salt, if needed, and more curry paste if you want a hotter curry. Before serving, roughly chop the cilantro leaves and throw them into the curry.

Pho is pretty much the perfect tonic to overstuffed Thanksgiving palates. It’s fresh, lively and deeply nourishing.

Turkey bones 2 onions halved and peeled A few fat slices of fresh ginger 5 star anise 2 cinnamon sticks 1 tsp fennel seeds 2 garlic cloves 1 Thai chil i, chopped 3 tbsp fish sauce 1 tbsp superfine or palm sugar

10 .5oz vermicelli rice noodles 10 .5oz leftover turkey, shredded A big handful of cilantro leaves A big handful of Thai basil or mint leaves 1 .75oz bean sprouts 6 lime wedges 4 Thai chil is, chopped Sriracha hot sauce (optional)

A few hours ahead: To make the broth, put a large, heavy-bottomed pot over the highest possible heat. Add the onion and the ginger. Burn them. Really burn them. Add the star anise, cinnamon, fennel seeds, garlic cloves, chili, turkey bones, fish sauce and sugar. Cover with water and bring to a boil. Simmer for 2–3 hours, until reduced by half. Strain and leave to cool, then chill, or continue to the next step. Cook the noodles according to package instructions, then cool in a bowl of iced water before draining.

30 minutes ahead: Put the broth over a medium heat. When hot, add the turkey to warm through. Taste the broth and add salt if necessary. Warm some large bowls.

To serve: Divide the noodles between the bowls. Spoon over the broth. Garnish with the herbs, bean sprouts, lime and chilis, and serve.

Winter on the east coast of Scotland can be bitingly cold. Hogmanay often saw our garden turned into an ice-bound realm beneath indigo skies. Going out was not much of an option, but there was little need as we devoured film after film, while the smells of Mum cooking turkey broth in the kitchen filled the air throughout the house.

While her brood hunkered under woolen blankets, Mum popped the carcass into a large pot with much chopped vegetables and a handful of barley, to be simmered for a fair few hours. The resulting broth was always the dish we craved most over the festivities.

1 roast turkey carcass 4 carrots 3 onions 6 celery stalks 1 small celery root (celeriac) 1 small rutabaga 4 slices bacon 4 bay leaves 2 sprigs each of thyme and savory 1 small bunch curly parsley, leaves picked and stems reserved 2 heaping tablespoons barley 2 large leeks 1 bunch scallions

Sit the carcass in a large pot. Peel and chop the carrots, onions, celery, celery root and rutabaga into smallish pieces. Cut the streaky bacon into small strips. Tie the bay leaves, thyme, savory and parsley stalks into a small bundle with twine.

Tumble all these into the pot with the turkey. Add the barley. Fill the pot with cold water and bring to a simmer over a gentle heat, spooning off any foam that rises to the surface. Leave the soup to tick over for 2 hours or so, until the barley and vegetables are tender. Turn the heat as low as can be and cook slowly for a further hour.

Trim the green part of the leek and chop into small pieces and chop the white of the leek into smallish squares also. Trim and slice the scallions thin. Wash these thoroughly and add to the soup 15 minutes before serving.

Chop the curly parsley leaves finely and add to the pot a minute before serving the soup. Bread and butter vital.

This is a super quick way to upcycle even a small amount of leftover meat into a special last-minute meal. If you don’t have hoisin sauce in the pantry, it’s possible you might have the ingredients to make your own – garlic, soy sauce, sweetener, vinegar, chil i of some sort and a blob of tahini or peanut butter are all you need to make it.

I really like the neutral flavor of Chinese-style pancakes, because it makes them a great carrier for other intense flavors, but if you can’t find them, regular wheat tortillas will work here instead.

1 tbsp vegetable oil , or sesame oil 3 garlic cloves , peeled and minced 2 tbsp soy sauce 2 tbsp black bean paste , or more soy sauce 3 tbsp sweetener – honey, sugar or molasses 3 tbsp vinegar – rice, white wine or apple cider vinegar 1 tbsp tahini , or creamy peanut butter 2 tsp sriracha , or gochujang or chili flakes ½ tsp Chinese five-spice powder

10 .5oz cooked turkey, shredded 1 tbsp vegetable oil , or sesame oil 4 tbsp hoisin sauce , plus extra to serve 12 Chinese-style pancakes 3.5oz cucumber , cut into matchsticks 3 scallions , trimmed and cut into matchsticks

To make your own hoisin sauce, heat the oil in a frying pan, then gently fry the garlic until it begins to turn light brown. Stir in the soy sauce, sweetener, vinegar, tahini and sriracha, then add the black bean paste and the five-spice. Bring to a boil, simmer for three minutes, then season to taste and leave to cool.

Put the oil in a frying pan over medium heat, add the shredded roast turkey and leave to cook without stirring until it’s crisp underneath. Break up the meat, stir in 3-4 tablespoons of hoisin sauce to coat it evenly, and cook for another minute.

Set the table with a platter of the crispy turkey, 12 steamed Chinese-style pancakes (or small tortillas), a bowl each of cucumber and scallions, and the hoisin sauce. To assemble a pancake, spread a little hoisin sauce on one side, top with some turkey, cucumber and scallion, then fold or roll and tuck in.

Chicken or ham work just as well instead of the turkey, if that’s what’s left over from yesterday’s menu. If you have more leftover meat, add more to the salad and increase the amount of dressing as needed.

7 oz cooked turkey, shredded 3 .5oz flat rice noodles (or mung bean noodles) ½ red onion, peeled and thinly sliced ¼ iceberg lettuce, cut into ¾in thick slices 2 medium carrots, peeled and julienned 0.75oz Thai basil leaves (or regular basil), torn 0.75oz mint leaves 1 .5oz cilantro leaves 3 .5oz bean sprouts 3 .5oz roasted salted peanuts, roughly chopped 3 red chil is, seeded and julienned 1 oz store-bought fried shallots

1 .75oz palm sugar, finely grated 1½ tbsp fish sauce 2 tbsp apple cider vinegar 2 tbsp lime juice, plus the finely grated zest of 1 lime 1½in piece fresh ginger, peeled and grated 1 tbsp soy sauce 2 tbsp peanut oil 1 garlic clove, peeled and crushed

Whisk all the ingredients for the dressing until the sugar has dissolved, and set aside.

Cook the noodles according to the package instructions (they vary from brand to brand). Drain, then put in a large serving bowl with all the remaining ingredients apart from the fried shallots. Pour over the dressing, toss gently, then take to the table or divide between six individual bowls. Serve, with the shallots sprinkled on top.

Normally, I prefer St Agur when cooking with blue cheese, but this recipe is perfect for using up stilton or any other leftover cheese. Walnuts combine deliciously here, as does the dash of brandy.

2 .25lb skinless cooked turkey meat 3 .5oz walnut pieces 3½ tbsp butter 2 tbsp chickpea flour 3¼ cups whole milk ½ small glass brandy 6 .5oz stilton or other blue cheese, crumbled 2 large garlic cloves, finely chopped 1 .75oz hard goat cheese

Preheat the oven to 340F. Cut the turkey into pieces and arrange in a large, fairly shallow ovenproof dish. Scatter the walnuts among the turkey.

Melt the butter in a fairly large saucepan, then remove from the heat, sift in the chickpea flour and stir in with a wooden spoon. Gradually stir in the milk and return to the heat. Bring up to bubbling, stirring all the time until the sauce is thick and smooth.

Still stirring, let it simmer gently for another 2–3 minutes. Then stir in the brandy, the crumbled stilton and the chopped garlic. Stir until the cheese has melted. Remove from the heat and add salt and pepper, to taste.

Pour the sauce over the turkey and walnuts. Coarsely grate the goat cheese and scatter it over the top. Cook in the center of the oven for 35–40 minutes, until it has turned a nice, golden brown.

Stir in a couple of chopped leeks if you’re not making the accompanying salad – soften them in butter first. And a word on that salad: don’t knock it until you’ve tried it. After all, if raw cabbage can work in a coleslaw …

14 oz roast turkey 3 .5oz ham 2 tbsp butter 2 tbsp all-purpose flour ⅔ cup chicken or turkey stock, or leftover gravy 1 cup milk 3 tbsp cream (heavy or half-and-half, whichever you have left over) 8 oz puff pastry All-purpose flour, to dust 1 egg, beaten

14 oz raw brussels sprouts, trimmed Handful of pecans, roughly chopped 6 tbsp olive oil 2 tbsp balsamic vinegar 3 tbsp fresh cranberry sauce Zest of ½ orange

Tear the turkey into evenly sized pieces, and roughly chop the ham. Preheat the oven to 356F.

Melt the butter in a medium saucepan over low heat, and stir in the flour. Cook, stirring, for a couple of minutes, then slowly whisk in the stock or gravy and the milk to make a smooth paste. Simmer gently for about 10 minutes until thickened, then add the cream and season to taste. Add the meat, and pour into a pie dish.

Roll out the pastry on a lightly floured surface until about ¼ inch thick, and brush the rim of the pie dish with beaten egg. Place the pastry on top, and press down around the rim, then trim off the excess – you can use these scraps to decorate the top of the pie if you like. Poke a hole in the middle to let the steam out, and brush with beaten egg.

Bake for about 30 minutes, until the pastry is golden and well puffed up.

Meanwhile, make the salad. Shred the sprouts finely, and place in a salad bowl with the pecans. Whisk together the oil and vinegar, then stir in the cranberry sauce and orange zest. Season well, and pour over the sprouts, then toss to coat. Serve alongside the pie.

paragraphs: Don’t settle for another turkey sandwich. Here are eight exciting ways to reinvent Thanksgiving leftovers
Download Feast , with more than 8,000 global recipes from Guardian chefs like Yotam Ottolenghi and Meera Sodha

T here’s only so much turkey sandwich a person can eat. Luckily, Thanksgiving leftovers are a delicious excuse to make something entirely new. From crispy hoisin pancakes to a fragrant turkey pho to a golden, cheesy gratin, here are eight ways to give yesterday’s bird a second life – or explore more recipes in our huge collection .
With a few vegetables and hours of gentle simmering, a turkey carcass becomes a golden stock for soups, pastas and anything you’re cooking in the weeks ahead.
1 cooked turkey carcass , with remaining skin and meat attached, stuffing removed 1 carrot 1 onion 1 celery stalk 2 bay leaves

Weigh the turkey carcass then put it in a large stockpot with the veg and bay leaves. Add about 2½ quarts of water for every pound of meat and bones. Put it on the lowest possible heat for a couple of hours. You’ll be left with a lovely stock for risotto, soups, or to freeze to use later.
Turkey meat is perfect for curries, and this recipe uses curry paste and quick-cook veg, so it takes no time at all to prepare and serve. Serve with a steaming mound of basmati rice.

2–2¼ lb skinless cooked turkey meat 1 lb zucchini 9 oz grape or cherry tomatoes 2 tbsp butter 2 tbsp canola oil 3-5 tsp tikka curry paste or mild curry paste 1 (13.5-oz) can coconut milk A handful of fresh cilantro leaves
Cut the cooked turkey meat into smallish pieces. Trim the ends of the zucchini and slice across fairly thinly. Halve the tomatoes lengthwise.

Heat the butter and oil in a large, deep pan over medium-high heat. When the butter has melted, add the zucchini and tomatoes and stir for 2–3 minutes, until the zucchini begins to soften but hasn’t lost its bite.
Next, add the curry paste and the sliced turkey. Stir over the heat for another minute or so.

Lastly, pour in the coconut milk, stir and bring just up to bubbling. Remove from the heat, add salt, if needed, and more curry paste if you want a hotter curry. Before serving, roughly chop the cilantro leaves and throw them into the curry.
Pho is pretty much the perfect tonic to overstuffed Thanksgiving palates. It’s fresh, lively and deeply nourishing.

10 .5oz vermicelli rice noodles 10 .5oz leftover turkey, shredded A big handful of cilantro leaves A big handful of Thai basil or mint leaves 1 .75oz bean sprouts 6 lime wedges 4 Thai chil is, chopped Sriracha hot sauce (optional)

A few hours ahead: To make the broth, put a large, heavy-bottomed pot over the highest possible heat. Add the onion and the ginger. Burn them. Really burn them. Add the star anise, cinnamon, fennel seeds, garlic cloves, chili, turkey bones, fish sauce and sugar. Cover with water and bring to a boil. Simmer for 2–3 hours, until reduced by half. Strain and leave to cool, then chill, or continue to the next step. Cook the noodles according to package instructions, then cool in a bowl of iced water before draining.
30 minutes ahead: Put the broth over a medium heat. When hot, add the turkey to warm through. Taste the broth and add salt if necessary. Warm some large bowls.
To serve: Divide the noodles between the bowls. Spoon over the broth. Garnish with the herbs, bean sprouts, lime and chilis, and serve.

Winter on the east coast of Scotland can be bitingly cold. Hogmanay often saw our garden turned into an ice-bound realm beneath indigo skies. Going out was not much of an option, but there was little need as we devoured film after film, while the smells of Mum cooking turkey broth in the kitchen filled the air throughout the house.

While her brood hunkered under woolen blankets, Mum popped the carcass into a large pot with much chopped vegetables and a handful of barley, to be simmered for a fair few hours. The resulting broth was always the dish we craved most over the festivities.

1 roast turkey carcass 4 carrots 3 onions 6 celery stalks 1 small celery root (celeriac) 1 small rutabaga 4 slices bacon 4 bay leaves 2 sprigs each of thyme and savory 1 small bunch curly parsley, leaves picked and stems reserved 2 heaping tablespoons barley 2 large leeks 1 bunch scallions

Sit the carcass in a large pot. Peel and chop the carrots, onions, celery, celery root and rutabaga into smallish pieces. Cut the streaky bacon into small strips. Tie the bay leaves, thyme, savory and parsley stalks into a small bundle with twine.

Tumble all these into the pot with the turkey. Add the barley. Fill the pot with cold water and bring to a simmer over a gentle heat, spooning off any foam that rises to the surface. Leave the soup to tick over for 2 hours or so, until the barley and vegetables are tender. Turn the heat as low as can be and cook slowly for a further hour.

Trim the green part of the leek and chop into small pieces and chop the white of the leek into smallish squares also. Trim and slice the scallions thin. Wash these thoroughly and add to the soup 15 minutes before serving.
Chop the curly parsley leaves finely and add to the pot a minute before serving the soup. Bread and butter vital.

This is a super quick way to upcycle even a small amount of leftover meat into a special last-minute meal. If you don’t have hoisin sauce in the pantry, it’s possible you might have the ingredients to make your own – garlic, soy sauce, sweetener, vinegar, chil i of some sort and a blob of tahini or peanut butter are all you need to make it.

I really like the neutral flavor of Chinese-style pancakes, because it makes them a great carrier for other intense flavors, but if you can’t find them, regular wheat tortillas will work here instead.

articles.content:
We scoured hundreds of sales for the best deals below $50 on heated blankets, packing cubes, sleep masks and more

B lack Friday deals aren’t reserved for pricey vacuum cleaners and huge TVs. While many of us gravitate toward big-ticket items with steep discounts, it is also worth searching for sales on smaller purchases, from reusable water bottles to phone chargers .

We combed through hundreds of deals to find 20 Black Friday deals under $50 worth a glance, from items for braving holiday travel to gift ideas rigorously tested by our editors.

We test products here at the Filter US and handpicked these deals. You can learn more about us at the bottom of the list. Products marked ( sold out ) are out of stock or no longer discounted. We’ll update our guides throughout Black Friday .

“Minuscule, lightweight and affordable, the Anker 511 Nano 3 (not to be confused with other 511 models) punches above its weight in a very crowded market,” said tech expert and tester Mark Knapp after testing 22 USB chargers . You can now grab it for $15% off.

Bedsure’s heated blanket was our favorite quick-to-heat blanket after testing two dozen . It took two minutes to start warming up, offering a welcome reprieve from the winter chill. Six heat settings let you find your ideal level of warmth, and its double-sided flannel and sherpa construction makes it extra snuggly. Best of all, it comes in 22 gift-worthy colors to suit anyone on your list, such as burgundy, which feels seasonally appropriate for the holidays.

Pack more than meets the eye with the compression packing cube set reviewer Les Shu appreciated for its ability to fit additional bulky garments on top of his testing load. “For the quality and performance you get at this price, these cubes are a great value,” he writes, awarding it the best for compression.

Don’t board your next long-haul flight without this compact wireless adapter . Filter contributor Sal Vaglica likes that it connects to in-flight entertainment systems via Bluetooth, adding “more versatility to the less tech-forward earbuds or over-ear headphones you already own”. Toss it in your carry-on while it’s 25% off.

$14 $25 at Amazon , Ulta Beauty Leading the charge in the K-beauty boom is this gentle yet mighty snail secretion serum designed to protect the skin’s barrier, hydrate and impart a lit-from-within “glass skin” look. I promise it’s not as gross as it sounds, and it absorbs instantly, leaving my skin feeling tighter and plumper. It’s also scent-free, which my sensitive skin appreciates.

Our best-tested sleep mask, after trying 32 models, is now 22% off. “The Mzoo’s main selling point is that it doesn’t give me what I think of as ‘facial claustrophobia’,” said tester Juno DeMelo of the sleep mask that delivers total darkness without pressure on your eyelids or your orbital bones.

The Owala FreeSip emerged victorious after we pitted it against a similar model from Yeti . While Yeti’s kept water cooler for longer, the Owala impressed contributor John Brandon with its well-designed spout and leakproof lid.

This weighted sleep mask is designed to provide gentle, soothing pressure without feeling too restrictive. It won over DeMelo, our resident sleep mask expert, who likened it to “a weighted blanket for your eyes”.

The tinned fish boom is sending pretty-packaged proteins to unprecedented highs, but with this Filter-favorite tuna in spicy olive oil , you can get in on the proteinmaxxing trend for 15% off, the lowest standard price we’ve seen this year. Steal Filter commissioning editor Karen Yuan’s idea and pair it with kimchi, sliced cucumber and dried seaweed flakes atop microwaved rice for an effortless dinner.

With this compact 20oz-ounce portable electric lunch box , now 25% off, you may finally have an excuse to skip that pricey and bland cafeteria lunch. “The Crock-Pot lunch box is perfect for bringing stewed lunches and soups to work in a cute, little portable container,” writes Filter contributor Jess Reyes.

Whether you’re desk-bound for work or catching a red-eye this holiday season, a three-pack of compression socks can help boost blood flow and circulation.“What I like most about these socks is the fit – snug without being uncomfortable on my calves with a cushioned sole,” said tester Latifah Muhammad in our compression sock guide .

$35 $170 at Amazon To keep tabs on all your Black Friday packages, you’ll want to upgrade that traditional doorbell to a video one. “ The Blink Battery Doorbell 2K+ remains excellent value for money,” writes tester Andy Shaw, highlighting its sharp daytime footage, clear two-way talk and intuitive app. Get it for 79% off.

$16 $21 at Amazon , Ulta Beauty Pat McGrath, a makeup artist and founder of the beauty brand Pat McGrath Labs, recommends this micellar water as a gentle makeup remover. “[It’s] the only cleanser I use backstage and on set because it’s made for the most sensitive skin and yet removes every trace of makeup, even waterproof,” she told Filter contributor Daisy Schofield.

Don’t skip the shades this winter: UV light reflects off snow, creating intense glare that can lead to a condition known as snow blindness, according to Johns Hopkins Medicine. “No matter how sweaty my face gets, the grip-coated frames never budge. They’re super snug and weigh just over half an ounce,” writes DeMelo, a CrossFit coach and Filter contributor, of Goodr’s polarized sunglasses . Get them for 25% off.

$13 $19 at Amazon While Yuan, the Filter’s commissioning editor, concedes that some toner pads are overhyped, Medicube’s, made with salicylic acid to unclog your pores, have won her over. “My skin has modestly but genuinely become clearer from using Medicube’s exfoliating pads ,” she said in her guide to the best Korean skincare . Stock up for 30% off.

If you’re prepping for a beach vacation this winter or stocking up before next summer, this dermatologist-approved, non-toxic mineral sunscreen is a great place to start. “Mineral sunscreens that use zinc oxide or titanium dioxide for sun protection are generally considered to be reef-safe,” Sapna Palep, MD, FAAD, MBA, a board-certified dermatologist, told Filter contributor Maria Ricapito in our best non-toxic sunscreen guide. Right now, it’s 20% off.

Ditch pricey pre-packaged salads, crudités and chips for homemade versions with this veggie chopper , now under $25 and 53% off. “I can just chuck in anything from the vegetable drawer (carrots, cucumber, peppers) and it all comes out in enticing cubes that [my kids] are happy to eat,” said Charlotte Northedge, a Guardian editor, in the Filter UK’s guide to products that save time and money .

Retinol can speed up cell turnover to help smooth fine lines and improve skin texture, writes beauty editor Sabine Wiesel. If you’re new to the ingredient, our favorite beginner-friendly eye serum from Beauty of Joseon is now 30% off. “The lightweight, silky serum is so gentle; I’ve seen no signs of irritation with daily use, just a smoother, firmer and brighter under-eye,” she writes. It’s now 30% off.

If you want to browse more Black Friday 2026 deals yourself, the links below lead directly to each major retailer’s holiday deals homepage. Check out our many buying guides and holiday gift guides for more ideas.

If you’re gifting, we have written guides to a lot of great, tested holiday gift picks at all price levels.

Advent calendar guides: The ‘Best’ , food , chocolate , coffee , beauty

We work for our readers, rather than the brands we write about. Every item we recommend is something a Filter editor or contributor has personally tested and can vouch for unless stated otherwise. On occasion, we may present a close substitute from the same brand and explain any differences from the original.

We scour competing retailers for the lowest prices on any item, and we use price-tracking tools such as Camelcamelcamel to check price history and ensure the discounts are truly good value, rather than a faux markdown. (So while we love sharing good deals, we also aren’t afraid to call out the unimpressive ones.)

Our mission is to help you filter out junk products and buy fewer, better things.

At the Filter US , we test the products we recommend ourselves and never take your trust for granted. We also consider possible impacts on your health or the environment in our coverage and companies cannot purchase a spot in our product rankings because we are here to serve you, not corporations.

Our dedicated testing, editing and production teams are based across the United States and Canada. We are a part of the Guardian’s US editorial team and our journalists follow its strict ethical standards. Learn more about us here .

articles.content:
I t’s an amazing moment when Anna Haugh lets me peel and chop a butternut squash, right there in the kitchen next to her, while she makes a beetroot pickle. The 46-year-old is a fiendish perfectionist and a fierce champion of every last ingredient. She’s making a dish that reflects the sensibility of her restaurant, Myrtle , named after the giant, dynastic wellspring of the Irish food scene, Myrtle Allen . It’s polenta with squash two ways – crushed and pureed – with pickle and goat’s cheese. Every ingredient has a story, and every story reaches back into an epic food tradition. There’s a lot going on, though you really have to see it to know just how much; so although I have the potential to really mess things up, here she has no choice but to let me peel and chop.

Elite cooking while talking like a Bren gun is a skill she’s honed, first in cookery demos “talking to a plastic bag and a stray dog, and you’d be lucky if someone came over to shelter from the rain”; then on Saturday Kitchen – a trial by fire: “Everything is easy after that. I could do any cookery programme now. I even tried to persuade them to do the MasterChef final live.”

Haugh grew up in Tallaght, a working-class suburb of Dublin, the youngest of four, her dad an engineer, her mother an incredible home cook who made everything from scratch, including things nobody ever makes, like cereal. “She taught us how to cook as a life skill,” says Haugh. “It was about nutrition and economy. Dad was the foodie.”

Being a chef just wasn’t a thing, she says – when Haugh told them of her ambitions at a careers meeting at school, the teacher “laughed and laughed – tears were coming out of her eyes – and she said, ‘Anna, you’ll be so sick of cooking after you get married.’” She went to the School of Culinary Arts and Food Technology in Dublin anyway, and her first apprenticeship was at the Salthill Hotel in Galway. When she walked into the kitchen, “for the first time in my life, I thought, ‘I belong here.’ I’d never felt anything like that before.” Her parents had always claimed that whatever Haugh and her three siblings wanted to do with their lives was fine by them, so long as they were happy. But her dad was appalled by her chosen vocation – she breaks into a heartfelt impression: “‘You’ve no workers’ rights, you won’t get holiday; when everyone else is having fun you’ll be working.’” He didn’t relent until 15 years later, when she was working for Gordon Ramsay.

In between she’d been at L’Ecrivain in Dublin when it got its first Michelin star under Derry Clarke; she’d gone to Paris, to work for Gualtiero Marchesi , the don of Italian nouvelle cuisine – “he used to eat buffalo mozzarella like an apple, with the milk dripping off his elbow.” She plainly had kitchen gifts – graft, curiosity, an incredible palate memory. In one kitchen they called her lagotto romagnolo – the truffle dog – because she’s like a nose-detective. The first solid advice she got, from a catering chef, pointed her in the right direction for the big leagues: “He said, repeat after me: ‘I want to go to a restaurant where you make everything homemade. Including the bread and the ice-cream.’”

She starts off making polenta, which takes an age because we’re cooking it, setting it, slicing it, dusting it, frying it. A lot of people, Haugh included, remember their first bad experience of polenta – a wet, grainy bed underneath some meat – but she’s determined to celebrate it – and not just because it’s good when it’s cooked properly. “Often it’s at the back of my mind: what is Irish food culture? Does it even exist? I was reading an old school book called Under the Hawthorne Tree, about the Irish famine, and they were always talking about yellow meal, which is polenta. When we arrived in America, people had starved on the journey – the ships would be full of dead people – so they called them coffin ships.” When the Native Americans, the Choctaw tribe in particular, heard about the famine, they gave money and polenta to the sailors to take back – it’s a particularly affecting moment in the solidarity of the colonised, because the Choctaw themselves had just suffered the forced displacement known as the Trail of Tears – but some other day for that gut-wrenching story. “I mightn’t be alive today if they hadn’t done that. So the idea that I can take polenta and elevate it in the restaurant, breathe some pride into what was a survival ingredient, is important.”

Polenta sets incredibly fast, and this story has only just begun when it has already been cooked with garlic and thyme, had cheese grated in, and put in a rounded mould to set. Nobody has to eat all this history in a chic, cheffy golden disc to comprehend its importance, but it does feel like a unique way to keep it alive. “There’s something in me that has to come out – a chef feels like that, a dancer feels like that. Sometimes in a job, you’re not paid a lot of money, but you’re giving what you should be giving, and that’s what creates meaning.”

People think pickles take for ever, because they mistake pickling for fermentation (and that really does take forever), but the onion and beetroot take no time at all, though if they’d had a whole day, everything would have been pinker still. As a chef and a restaurateur, Haugh toggles naturally between no-bullshit pragmatism and poetry. She describes her philosophy on veganism and you think, veggies must have waited a lifetime for a high-end chef like this. “When I was training, vegetarianism was thought of as just a fad, and there was a lot of chicken and fish stock in vegetarian soup. Then, when veganism came in, people were treating it like the new vegetarianism, but I thought: ‘This isn’t going away. You get on this choo-choo train now or later.’”

At Myrtle, they can make their tasting menu completely vegan with no notice, and Haugh takes pride in that. “A langoustine is quite easy to make outstanding, but a carrot or an onion – that takes skill. That’s what it’s all about.”

More surprising still, “You can come to the restaurant and say: ‘I don’t like red peppers.’ You don’t have to explain why – maybe it makes you burp or fart. You’re allowed to say: ‘I don’t want red peppers in my food.’” That’s very much the persona she brings to the screen – fun, unpretentious, relatable – although the relaxed vibe that comes across on Masterchef was quite hard won, she says. “When I was on Hell’s Kitchen, I lost the ability to talk. It’s in this big Bel Air mansion, and I’m with Wolfgang Puck and the two famous Nancys , these fucking legends, right? And I’m tasting the dishes, and all I could said repeatedly was: ‘It’s elicious. It’s elicious. Needs salt. Elicious.’ I was blind with nerves.”

But if she’s not precious, her menus are incredibly considered and – she’d probably scoff at this – political. They have a dish called Siobhan’s Quest, named after the maker of Saint Tola goat’s cheese, Siobhán Ní Gháirbhith, who went on a crusade against the government and EU when they tried to ban unpasteurised cheese to appeal to the US export market. There’s another dish called Newgrange , inspired by the ancient site in Ireland: “One day of the year, on the solstice, the sun lights up the entire thing, the rest of the year it’s in darkness.” The dish also came about from constantly clashing with an under-chef who wanted to make more dishes that were Asian-infused. “You don’t want to squash the flame of creativity, but you’re also thinking: it’s an Irish restaurant, about Irish stories, Irish ingredients, Irish culture.” Somehow, out of this battle of wills, came this salad of carrageen moss, Cashel Blue cheese and other Waldorf salad ingredients arranged on a walnut biscuit, to represent Newgrange: “Everybody likes apples, pears, walnuts, blue cheese. But people also love that place.”

To come back to that question, is there an Irish food culture, and if so, what is it? This dish that’s coming together today – the earthy orange and yellow hues of vegetable and yellow meal, broken up by bright and translucent pink pickle, crunchy pumpkin seeds and Jerusalem artichoke – couldn’t look more modern, and yet couldn’t be more rooted in Ireland’s food history.

“This is just a makey-uppy Anna theory – but youse had some lad who took over … William the Conqueror? Well, he introduced worshipping the French. He looked down on British culture, and it stunted the evolution of British cuisine. And that’s why it isn’t like French or Italian, because even though all of their foods originated with peasant dishes, too, they were then elaborated. Ireland is similar with colonial rule.

“This is obviously a very sensitive subject,” she says – and I worry that she’s going to be careful with her words – “but during colonial rule, we were told that anything Irish was shit. That’s how you control a country. Then, when we got our freedom around 1921, we had to reintroduce our language. And we had to reintroduce our cuisine as well. All the bits that you might think are boring – that’s Irish food, but it just hasn’t evolved yet. That’s fruit cake, apple tart, spiced beef, honey glazed ham, mackerel with oats ...” It doesn’t sound at all boring, as she rattles it off; you’d eat it simple, and you’d eat it complicated, and for the chef doing centuries of elaboration at breakneck speed, all you can do is stand back, peel her a butternut squash, and await her next move.

Haugh first unveiled her spike as she darted it elegantly into some frying whole garlic cloves to check their softness. It’s silver, about the length of an Agatha Christie hatpin, has a little ball at one end (though that’s just decorative), and it’s the simplest and most versatile piece of equipment I’ve ever seen. She uses it on vegetables, and you could presumably use it on a cake to check it comes out clean, but she also uses it as a temperature probe.

If you jab it into meat or fish and know what you’re doing, you can tell whether they’re done by holding it under your bottom lip. “You can feel on your skin whether it’s 65 degrees or 50.” Checking a lasagne, “which should be boiling”, she’ll hold it against her hand so she doesn’t burn herself. “You can use a temperature probe, but that might break in the middle of a service,” is one rationale, but another is that the personal satisfaction of building a thermometer with nothing but your own skin and knowledge is immense. “When you use this, you feel like you’re cooking. When you use a temperature probe, you feel like a chemist. There’s not a single chef I’ve ever taught this to who doesn’t use it.”

Jerusalem artichoke is a magic ingredient. Slice it with a mandoline and deep-fry it, and you have vegetable crisps that will ruin an old school crisp-fan’s palate – the potato will never taste as good again. Crush and sprinkle them through mashed root vegetables, and they mix up the texture in a fascinating way; braise them along with the squash or carrot for a deeper flavour. They turn a soup into a main event. “It’s like lovage, you know; use a tiny bit and it elevates everything.”

Golden beetroot isn’t just a posh-looking beetroot – Haugh adds turmeric when she’s pickling and it brings out “an almost fruity note, another layer of flavour”. Sometimes she dusts it in cinnamon, and the combination is so particular, sweet and warm.

For the pickled pearl onions 100g red-wine vinegar 50g sugar 1 tsp salt 10 pearl onions, peeled and cut in half 1 small raw beetroot (60-80g) , peeled and sliced thinly

For the polenta 2 garlic cloves, peeled and cut in half 3 sprigs of thyme 2 tbsp extra-virgin olive oil, plus extra for frying 5g salt 100g quick-cook polenta, plus extra for dusting 20g unsalted butter 50g Cais Na Tire or pecorino, grated St Tola’s goat’s cheese, crumbled, to serve

For the butternut crush 300g butternut squash, peeled and chopped 2 Jerusalem artichokes, peeled and sliced Olive oil (about 40ml) 2 generous pinche s of salt 2 tbsp toasted pumpkin seeds 1 bunch basil leaves, the majority ripped, plus a few leaves left whole to serve 30g unsalted butter (optional)

For the butternut puree 2 cinnamon sticks, chopped 1 tbsp olive oil 300g butternut squash, peeled and chopped Sea salt 50g double cream

For the pickled onions, put the vinegar, 100ml water, the sugar and salt in a pan and bring to a boil. Add the pearl onions, bring back to the boil, then add the beetroot, turn off the heat, and leave to cool for at least 30 minutes. This will then keep for weeks in the fridge.

To make the polenta, sweat the garlic and thyme in the olive oil, then add 500ml water and the salt, and bring to a boil.

Whisk in the polenta and turn the heat to a medium. Once bubbling, add the butter and grated cheese, stirring constantly.

Pour into a loaf tin (I used a large, round plastic cup) and set aside for 30 minutes to cool. Transfer to the fridge until completely cold – one to two hours.

Heat the oven to 200C (180C fan)/390F/gas 6. To make the squash crush, toss the squash and artichoke with the oil and salt, and roast for 15 minutes, until soft. Crush with a fork. Add the toasted pumpkin seeds and the ripped basil leaves – they really complement the butternut. You can add the butter, if you feel it needs it. Taste for salt.

To make the squash puree, toast the cinnamon in a pan with the olive oil over a medium heat, then add the squash and a generous pinch of salt.

Cover with 100ml water and simmer until soft – about 15 minutes. Transfer to a blender with the cream, and blend until super smooth.

Cut the set polenta into about one inch-thick slices and dust with polenta. Fry the polenta in oil in a frying pan on a medium heat, until golden brown on each side.

To serve, spoon the puree on to plates, then top with the fried polenta. Spoon the butternut crush on top, crumble over some goat’s cheese, and garnish with the basil leaves and pickled pearl onions.

To make the polenta, sweat the garlic and thyme in the olive oil, then add 500ml water and the salt, and bring to a boil.
Whisk in the polenta and turn the heat to a medium. Once bubbling, add the butter and grated cheese, stirring constantly.
Pour into a loaf tin (I used a large, round plastic cup) and set aside for 30 minutes to cool. Transfer to the fridge until completely cold – one to two hours.

Heat the oven to 200C (180C fan)/390F/gas 6. To make the squash crush, toss the squash and artichoke with the oil and salt, and roast for 15 minutes, until soft. Crush with a fork. Add the toasted pumpkin seeds and the ripped basil leaves – they really complement the butternut. You can add the butter, if you feel it needs it. Taste for salt.
To make the squash puree, toast the cinnamon in a pan with the olive oil over a medium heat, then add the squash and a generous pinch of salt.
Cover with 100ml water and simmer until soft – about 15 minutes. Transfer to a blender with the cream, and blend until super smooth.
Cut the set polenta into about one inch-thick slices and dust with polenta. Fry the polenta in oil in a frying pan on a medium heat, until golden brown on each side.
To serve, spoon the puree on to plates, then top with the fried polenta. Spoon the butternut crush on top, crumble over some goat’s cheese, and garnish with the basil leaves and pickled pearl onions.

articles.content:
There is cynicism and jealousy but one of County’s top scorers is 39 as club try to climb leagues again after tumbling

I t was a vidiprinter moment worthy of a double take. Ross County 1 Cove Rangers 1 (Keir 52). Would Cove, scrapping for survival in Scottish League One, put an unlikely end last Saturday to the most emphatic run in British senior football? Don’t be silly, retorted County; four goals in the closing 17 minutes extended the Dingwall side’s goal difference to plus 45 (for 56, against 11). Played 16, won 14, drawn two. There is as much chance of Mike McCarthy settling down for Christmas dinner with Aaron Rodgers as there is of County missing out on promotion back to Scotland’s second tier. Taking in cup competitions they have scored 102 goals this season.

An assessment from the captain, Brian Graham, of a frankly irrelevant loss on penalties to Stenhousemuir in the Challenge Cup epitomises the County approach. “We should have been five- or six-nil up at half-time,” an irked Graham says. “That shows the standards we have set. We lost a dubious goal, which shouldn’t have stood.” Earlier in that competition County whacked 14 past a Hearts youth side before defeating a Celtic B team including two Chelsea loanees and a £3m midfielder.

Unsurprisingly there is cynicism, laced with jealousy, about County’s position. They are portrayed as wild spenders in a frugal environment. A club in the wrong competitive domain. The analysis does not stack up. Graham, the scorer of 21 goals across all competitions, is 39. The prominent Adam Emslie was last on loan at Cove after being rejected by Aberdeen. Luke McCarvel arrived via Kelty Hearts and Cumbernauld Colts. Lewis Reid is previously of Stranraer, Lewis Strapp a signing from Airdrie. County have a batch of Scottish Championship-capable players, not Premiership-ready ones. Their form is still extraordinary.

“People don’t know the ins and outs of this club,” says Graham. “I speak to the chief executive – as the captain I need to work on the bonuses – and I can see a massive difference now to what it was previously. There’s not players on wages like the exaggeration of what people say they are on. People just play guessing games. But look at Scottish football as a whole; budgets do not give you the right to win matches anyway. It’s players on the pitch who have to do it.

“If you had said to me I would have 21 goals in November, I would have laughed at you. I had a number in my black book which I have exceeded. I now have another number in there.” Not that wider records – 100 goals, 100 points or an unbeaten league campaign – are viewed similarly. “We haven’t spoken about that,” Graham says. “We are getting a lot of plaudits, a lot of people speaking about it, but the manager insists we keep our feet on the ground and don’t listen to outside noise. When you put yourself in the position we have, teams are desperate to beat us.”

Only Boreham Wood, with 16 wins and three draws from 19 National League games and 53 goals scored, are in touching distance of County’s win percentage. Graham is ideally placed to speak on County’s journey. Now in spell three, he played for them in the top flight and when Hibernian were vanquished in the League Cup final of 2016. A club who had been a small Highland League team in the early 1990s were giving bloody noses to the big boys. Subsequent years brought trauma, culminating in successive demotions from 2025. County kept faith in the summer with their manager, Stuart Kettlewell. Graham returned to spearhead a fightback. Pre-season games, which began in late June, included a comprehensive closed-doors win over Aberdeen.

“The manager had to build a new squad and bring in younger players,” Graham says. “The manager has created a new culture that he spoke to me about before I came in. We had to get back to basics, everybody wanting to train every day and fight for their jersey. He has created that environment; nobody is resting on their laurels and everyone is pulling their weight. The manager and coaching staff have really high standards, which the players know about. Nobody gets away with any nonsense.”

The emphasis on attitude is apposite. County have a generous owner and, owing to geographical location, were always known to pay decent salaries to prise players from the central belt. In recent times, received wisdom was that players were using the club for a payday that came free from accountability. The team spiralled as a result, having previously brought wider attention on Dingwall and boosted the local economy.

“It is a community club, a family club,” says Graham. “We have excellent volunteers. One woman comes in every week with her spaniel – I think the dog likes the pies – to help clean the stands but she is not the only one. You want to come to your work because there are good people here.

“At the start of the season the fans were a bit dejected, the numbers weren’t quite there. Slowly but surely people are coming back to support us, they realise this is a team to get behind. It’s a real Ross County side, people willing to fight for the jersey, which is what this club is all about.”

On Saturday County host Brora Rangers in the Scottish Cup. While not quite a derby – the towns are almost 50 miles apart – this is a compelling fixture. Brora look capable of leaping from the Highland League to the Scottish League, as County did in 1994. Graham wants a cup run to bring finance into a business which has had to withstand sharp income drops. There is a more endearing cause. Bobby Wilson, who presided over County’s league entry having scaled European highs when a player with Dundee, died on 18 November. A celebration of Wilson’s life will soon take place at County’s home. He would approve of this resurgence.
