articles.title: England beat Australia by seven wickets: third men’s Twenty20 international – as it hapened
articles.summary: Australia collapse to their worst T20i total at home as England race to seven-wicket win at the Gabba 4th over: Australia 39-1 (Fraser-McGurk 4, Harper 24) Harry Brook turns to pace in the form of Henry Crocombe. A top edge from Harper is meaty enough to fly for SIX over the keeper’s head but it’s a decent over from Crocombe who responds with pace and bounce, beating the bat a couple of times. Nine off the over. 3rd over: Australia 30-1 (Fraser-McGurk 2, Harper 17) Sam Harper opens the shoulders at the Gabba! Coles continues, his first ball is smashed down the ground for SIX. Coles drags down and Harper slams four through the leg side. Pressure on the young Coles here… SIX! Harper backs away to give himself room to blast another big one down the ground. Australia hit back. Continue reading...
articles.content:
That’s it from me today. Ali Martin’s report from the Gabba will be along any moment. We’ll be back for the fourth game from Sydney on Sunday, do join us for that.

“Very disappointing. We’ve got to own that. The Gabba is an excellent place to bat and some of our shot selection was off tonight. I don’t want this young group to fear making mistakes but tonight was a chance to be a bit more calculated. So, no excuses, we’ve got to be better.”

You see it a lot in T20 cricket, you think you need 200 to win the game but you can overplay that and get in trouble. We’ve all played Big Bash games here, got to give yourself the chance to cash in at the back end. We didn’t get near that tonight. Still excited about the talent in the group. Tonight was disappointing but still two days (matches) to go.”

Mitch Marsh staggers off with a hundred yard stare. A look that sums up Australian cricket at this moment in time.

England were slick this evening, Jamie Overton’s five-fer setting up the game and Donald and Cox impressing once again with the bat in the chase of a small target.

“The last couple of games I’ve been disappointed with the way I’ve bowled, we haven’t got a few experienced players here so it was a chance to step up and it’s nice to put in a performance today.

I try to contribute in the field and get in those hot spots. Maybe that helped today! We’ve done a lot of fitness and it’s paying off at the moment but we’ll keep working on it and try to be the fittest team we can be.”

Ben Dwarshius is into the attack, his first ball is kablammoed back at him by Banton, it has to go down as a drop but actually the bowler did well to get his fingers up and protect his face. In fact, the replays show that the ball did indeed hit Dwashuis on the top of the head after bursting through his fingers. Yikes. He’s checked over and good to continue.

Jordan Cox! Stop it! Three consecutive fours smoked by the ginger tyro!

England need 7 runs to win and the Gabba ground staff try to bring the covers on with rain falling… surely not? Nope, the umpires decide that it is a madness at this stage in proceedings and send them on their way. Cricket , eh?

Still, the time delay means they lose another over and England need just two more runs to win.

There it is! Cox strokes for two and England take the win to go 2-1 up in the five match series. You know what, I think I might just be ‘whelmed’ by the end to that game.

8th over: England 78-3 (Banton 9, Cox 19) Jordan Cox shows his flair with a pull for SIX over midwicket and two further fours into the leg side. Billy Stanlake might wish he didn’t bowl through, 17 runs coming off his fourth over. England need just 20 more now.

7th over: England 61-3 (Banton 8, Cox 4) Shot! Banton drives a crisp four through cover and then rotates strike with a clip off his pads to the leg side. DROP! Oh and that’s a bad miss. Chaudhary spills the chance at backward point to gift Cox a life. Australia cannot afford to give England lives, the sharpness between sides in the field has been very apparent in this series so far.

Here we go again, England need 45 more from 66 balls . Riley Meredith is going to bowl his fourth over on the bounce. Cox and Banton at the crease.

Thankfully the covers are currently being peeled off for the second time, we should be back on in just over five minutes. The game has been reduced to a 17 over match so there will be a revised target.

6th over: England 53-3 (Banton 3, Cox 1) Marsh sticks with his quicks. Stanlake is short and in at the ribs, nasty stuff. He then pushes one fuller and beats Cox’s on the outside edge. Smart cricket from Banton and Cox who pick off the singles, there’s no need for them to go down in a blaze here with only 56 runs needed.

That’s the end of the powerplay oh flip, here comes the rain and covers again.

5th over: England 49-3 (Banton 1, Cox 0) Jordan Cox defends his first ball to see out Meredith’s over, it’s one that has given the Aussies a glimmer of hope with both Brook and Donald back in the hutch.

Two in the over for Riley Meredith! A slower ball outside off stump is guided straight to point by Donald. England aren’t home yet…

Brook is caught by a diving Mitch Marsh running back at mid off! He tried to combat the pace and bounce but the ball hit high on the blade. Tom Banton joins Donald in the middle.

4th over: England 46-1 (Donald 31, Brook 8) Billy Stanlake has one ball left to bowl in the fourth over. He sends down a zippy bouncer that follows Harry Brook down the leg side, Brook just manages to get his grille inside the line and falls over as he succesfully avoids getting pinned. Nasty ball from Stanlake to resume proceedings and finish the over.

Good news! The rain has stopped, the rope has been dragged and the players are heading back out at the Gabba. England need 64 more runs to go 2-1 up in the five match series.

Gah! Just as Aneurin Donald was beginning to put on another show the heavens open in Brisbane and on come the covers. We don’t currently have enough overs in the bank to call it a game either, that requires five overs of England’s response and they’ve only had 3.5 so far.

Dang and blast. Hopefully the wet stuff moves through and we can at least get an official result. Donald has 31 off 11 balls, he’d just blitzed three consecutive fours off Stanlake.

3rd over: England 32-1 (Donald 18, Brook 8) What a shot from Harry Brook! He digs out a full ball from Meredith and somehow it soars flat like an exocet over cover for SIX! He does it all time time and every time it leaves the jaw on the floor. Remarkable.

“On no!” cries Salt as he is beaten for pace by Stanlake and plinks an easy catch into the off side. England lose their first and it brings captain Harry Brook to the middle. Do not adjust your set.

2nd over: England 22-0 (Salt 3, Donald 18) Donald crouches in his stance and keeps his eyes trained on the ball, leaning into a drive that somehow soars over midwicket for SIX! He didn’t time that at all but the power he has made it not matter a jot. Donald backs away to the next ball and carves over point for four.

1st over: England 9-0 (Salt 1, Donald 8) Salt clips off his pads to get England going. Donald then open his account with flick off his hip fine for four. The ball skids on a touch, Donald tries to launch over cover but doesn’t time it. The Welshman is very much in the shop window for lucrative franchise gigs, India’s wunderkind Vaibhav Sooryavanshi is the only ‘man’ striking the white ball better than him at the moment.

Close! Donald mis-times a pull and it goes high into the leg side but Billy Stanlake slips over haring in to take the catch! That’s a life for Nye.

Here come Salt and Donald. Riley Meredith will start with the ball for Australia, the home side need to make early inroads. Play!

Jamie Overton speaks briefly to the broadcaster after his fantastic 5-12 with the ball. They are the *second-best figures for an Englishman in T20 internationals.

*Go on then – Sam Curran took 5-10 against Afghanistan in the 2022 World Cup. You knew that.

“I hadn’t been bowling well in the first two games, a bit short and a bit erratic. I tried to work on doing the basics well, smashing the top of the stumps.”

Here come England for their response, we might not be here very long BUT YOU NEVER KNOW.

Sam Curran bowls Billy Stanlake and with that subjects Australia to their lowest ever total in T20I cricket.

England have been excellent, razor sharp and clinical. Dare I say it, ruthless .

Bad to worse. Mitch Owen was the man who could have biffed a few boundaries but he has a brain fade and runs himself out attempting a second run that did not exist.

16th over: Australia 108-8 (Owen 16, Meredith 0) Australia are in the mire, Riley Meredith plays out a wicket maiden from Liam Dawson.

Liam Dawson comes back into the attack and Adam Zampa struggles to lay a bat on him… surviving a tight lbw call on review but his slightly tortured innings comes to a close with a nick behind two balls later. Jordan Cox taking a sharp catch behind the sticks.

15th over: Australia 107-7 (Owen 16, Zampa 3) What can Australia muster? Henry Crocombe comes back into the attack, Owen pumps a full ball for four down the ground and then swings a SIX away over the leg side to provide a welcome shot in the arm to Australia’s total.

14th over: Australia 94-7 (Owen 5, Zampa 1) Overton finished with a wicket-maiden and winds up with a brilliant 5-12 from his four overs. He’s single-handedly set England up for victory at the Gabba. Adam Zampa is at the crease for Australia as his fellow spinner Adil Rashid finishes his spell with 0-17. Miserly.

Can Overton pick up a lesser spotted T20I five fer? The Aussies look like they are trying to see him off, Ben Dwarshius is the new batter and he plays out three dots. One ball to come from Overton… there it is! Dwarshius drives and nicks behind! Scenes at the Gabba as Jamie Overton becomes only the second English player to bag a T20I five-fer!

Jamie Overton is playing a blinder! The big man is smashed on the hand off his first ball as he fails to cling onto rasping return catch but he shrugs it off to see the end of Chaudhary with his next ball! Caught a long on, Australia imploding.

12th over: Australia 92-5 (Chaudhary 19, Owen 4) England squeeeeze at the Gabba, Rashid whistles through his third and it only costs two runs. Overton is indeed going to bowl through, here he comes for his fourth.

11th over: Australia 90-5 (Chaudhary 18, Owen 3) Spencer Johnson Mitch Owen comes in for Australia, England sense blood in the water. Jamie Overton has 3-12 from his three overs. He might bowl straight through here too.

Guess who!? Jamie Overton has been involved in all of the dismissals today and he gets the third to his name after bouncing out Joel Davies!

10th over: Australia 86-4 (Chaudhary 17, Davies 3) Rashid again, Chaudhary stays in his own bubble with wickets falling around him, a tidy reverse bring him four. Three singles makes it seven off the over, that’s the halfway stage and England will be very happy with how they are placed. Australia have a longer tail today after choosing to go in with an extra bowler, they might come to regret that decision.

9th over: Australia 79-4 (Chaudhary 11, Davies 2) Joel Davies joins Chaudhary and Australia need to rebuild. Drop! The new man is nearly on his way first ball but Rashid can’t take the diving effort at backward point. Has to go down as a drop but it was a tough one. Still, England on top at the Gabba.

Gone! David tries to pull Overton but doesn’t get enough of it, Henry Crocombe clinging on in the deep. David has a glance at the pitch as he departs but there are no demons there, he was done by cross seam delivery from Overton.

8th over: Australia 71-3 (Chaudhary 11, David 6) Adil Rashid into the attack and he whizzes through a cheap over for England, just six runs off it.

7th over: Australia 71-3 (Chaudhary 6, David 5) Tim David strides to the middle. We all know what he is capable of but England will be buoyed by the three wickets that keep Australia in check. Ouch! Chaudhary is clanged on the helmet by a short one and there’s a brief delay while he is checked over. He’s good to continue and watches David pull the final ball of the over for four.

You can’t keep Jamie Overton out of the action! Brook brings the big fella into the attack and he strikes with a cross seam delivery that JFM tries to launch down the ground… only to find the safe hands of Tom Banton.

6th over: Australia 64-2 (Fraser-McGurk 22, Chaudhary 5) Nikil Chaudhary joins JFM in the middle at the Gabba. He has a look at Dawson for a couple of balls and then sweeps with confidence for four. A clip of the toes brings Fraser-McGurk on strike and he ends the over with a flick for four over wide mid on. Decent contest this, honours around even at the end of the powerplay.

England needed that. Harper plinks a top edge to bucket hands Overton at mid on.

5th over: Australia 55-1 (Fraser-McGurk 18, Harper 26) Sam Curran enters the fray with his bag of tricks. Jake Fraser-McGurk hasn’t had many ball so far and he makes up for it by clubbing two remarkable sixes off the over! A flat batted pull flies over mid on and is followed by an astounding sort of flicked pull over the leg side. Welcome to the party.

4th over: Australia 39-1 (Fraser-McGurk 4, Harper 24) Harry Brook turns to pace in the form of Henry Crocombe. A top edge from Harper is meaty enough to fly for SIX over the keeper’s head but it’s a decent over from Crocombe who responds with pace and bounce, beating the bat a couple of times. Nine off the over.

3rd over: Australia 30-1 (Fraser-McGurk 2, Harper 17) Sam Harper opens the shoulders at the Gabba! Coles continues, his first ball is smashed down the ground for SIX. Coles drags down and Harper slams four through the leg side. Pressure on the young Coles here… SIX! Harper backs away to give himself room to blast another big one down the ground. Australia hit back.

2nd over: Australia 14-1 (Fraser-McGurk 2, Harper 1) Sam Harper arrives in the middle, he can hit a long ball. Dawson rattles through his over and England will be very happy with their start.

Spin from both ends to start at the Gabba. Liam Dawson has the second over and removes Marsh with his second ball! Marsh tried to smear into the leg side but an under edge saw the ball plink to Overton at midwicket, the big man swooping to take a good low catch. Early breakthrough for England.

1st over: Australia 7-0 (Marsh 7, Fraser-McGurk 0) The dashing James Coles starts with the new white ball for England, three dots to start and a frisson round the ground. Bang! Marsh has a look and then lofts a straight SIX down the ground to open Australia’s account. The Aussie skipper doesn’t look too comfortable against the spin though and there’s only one more single to add to the six off the over.

Good news from the ground, there were a few umbrellas up in the Brisbane mizzle but it’s a negligible miasma at the moment. The covers are off and the players are heading out there as I type.

The broadened timeline also includes the preceding Ashes series, amid accusations that Australian players had also tampered with the ball before the tour to South Africa.

England harboured suspicions about Australia’s ball maintenance methods during that 4-0 Ashes defeat, not least during the final day of the third Test in Perth when the hosts got the ball to reverse despite damp conditions caused by a significant a rain delay that morning.

Alastair Cook then went on to detail an alleged dressing room exchange with David Warner at the end of the series in his 2019 autobiography – a claim also made by Chris Woakes in his recently published memoir.

Cook wrote : “Warner, a couple of beers into his celebration, mentioned that he used substances attached to the strapping on his hand to accelerate the deterioration of the ball during a first-class match. I looked at Steve Smith who shot a glance that said: ‘Ooh, you shouldn’t have said that.’”

In an interview with Sky Sports this week, Khawaja claimed ball tampering was occuring before the South Africa tour. “What we were doing wasn’t within the laws of the game,” he added.

Harry Brook calls the coin correctly and inserts Mitch Marsh’s Australia with a bit of pesky weather around in Brisbane, hopefully we’ll start on time.

England are unchanged from the previous match while Marsh confirms that Mitch Owen and Billy Stanlake are back in the side for this one.

Australia 1 Mitchell Marsh (c), 2 Jake Fraser-McGurk, 3 Sam Harper (wk), 4 Nikhil Chaudhary, 5 Tim David, 6 Joel Davies, 7 Mitchell Owen, 8 Ben Dwarshuis, 9 Adam Zampa, 10 Riley Meredith, 11 Billy Stanlake

England 1 Phil Salt, 2 Aneurin Donald, 3 Harry Brook (c), 4 Tom Banton, 5 James Coles, 6 Sam Curran, 7 Jordan Cox (wk), 8 Liam Dawson, 9 Jamie Overton, 10 Adil Rashid, 11 Henry Crocombe

“I’m pretty decent at slogging it, and not too good at batting, so I’ll keep swinging as hard as I can!”

Donald hit nine big ones (and four fours) to make 85 off 32 balls, the Welshman’s innings leaving his captain Harry Brook “speechless” afterwards.

paragraphs: That’s it from me today. Ali Martin’s report from the Gabba will be along any moment. We’ll be back for the fourth game from Sydney on Sunday, do join us for that.

“Very disappointing. We’ve got to own that. The Gabba is an excellent place to bat and some of our shot selection was off tonight. I don’t want this young group to fear making mistakes but tonight was a chance to be a bit more calculated. So, no excuses, we’ve got to be better.”

You see it a lot in T20 cricket, you think you need 200 to win the game but you can overplay that and get in trouble. We’ve all played Big Bash games here, got to give yourself the chance to cash in at the back end. We didn’t get near that tonight. Still excited about the talent in the group. Tonight was disappointing but still two days (matches) to go.”
Mitch Marsh staggers off with a hundred yard stare. A look that sums up Australian cricket at this moment in time.
England were slick this evening, Jamie Overton’s five-fer setting up the game and Donald and Cox impressing once again with the bat in the chase of a small target.
“The last couple of games I’ve been disappointed with the way I’ve bowled, we haven’t got a few experienced players here so it was a chance to step up and it’s nice to put in a performance today.

I try to contribute in the field and get in those hot spots. Maybe that helped today! We’ve done a lot of fitness and it’s paying off at the moment but we’ll keep working on it and try to be the fittest team we can be.”

In fact, the replays show that the ball did indeed hit Dwashuis on the top of the head after bursting through his fingers. Yikes. He’s checked over and good to continue.
Jordan Cox! Stop it! Three consecutive fours smoked by the ginger tyro!

England need 7 runs to win and the Gabba ground staff try to bring the covers on with rain falling… surely not? Nope, the umpires decide that it is a madness at this stage in proceedings and send them on their way. Cricket , eh?
Still, the time delay means they lose another over and England need just two more runs to win.
There it is! Cox strokes for two and England take the win to go 2-1 up in the five match series. You know what, I think I might just be ‘whelmed’ by the end to that game.

8th over: England 78-3 (Banton 9, Cox 19) Jordan Cox shows his flair with a pull for SIX over midwicket and two further fours into the leg side. Billy Stanlake might wish he didn’t bowl through, 17 runs coming off his fourth over. England need just 20 more now.

7th over: England 61-3 (Banton 8, Cox 4) Shot! Banton drives a crisp four through cover and then rotates strike with a clip off his pads to the leg side. DROP! Oh and that’s a bad miss. Chaudhary spills the chance at backward point to gift Cox a life. Australia cannot afford to give England lives, the sharpness between sides in the field has been very apparent in this series so far.
Here we go again, England need 45 more from 66 balls . Riley Meredith is going to bowl his fourth over on the bounce. Cox and Banton at the crease.

Thankfully the covers are currently being peeled off for the second time, we should be back on in just over five minutes. The game has been reduced to a 17 over match so there will be a revised target.

6th over: England 53-3 (Banton 3, Cox 1) Marsh sticks with his quicks. Stanlake is short and in at the ribs, nasty stuff. He then pushes one fuller and beats Cox’s on the outside edge. Smart cricket from Banton and Cox who pick off the singles, there’s no need for them to go down in a blaze here with only 56 runs needed.
That’s the end of the powerplay oh flip, here comes the rain and covers again.

5th over: England 49-3 (Banton 1, Cox 0) Jordan Cox defends his first ball to see out Meredith’s over, it’s one that has given the Aussies a glimmer of hope with both Brook and Donald back in the hutch.
Two in the over for Riley Meredith! A slower ball outside off stump is guided straight to point by Donald. England aren’t home yet…
Brook is caught by a diving Mitch Marsh running back at mid off! He tried to combat the pace and bounce but the ball hit high on the blade. Tom Banton joins Donald in the middle.

4th over: England 46-1 (Donald 31, Brook 8) Billy Stanlake has one ball left to bowl in the fourth over. He sends down a zippy bouncer that follows Harry Brook down the leg side, Brook just manages to get his grille inside the line and falls over as he succesfully avoids getting pinned. Nasty ball from Stanlake to resume proceedings and finish the over.
Good news! The rain has stopped, the rope has been dragged and the players are heading back out at the Gabba. England need 64 more runs to go 2-1 up in the five match series.

Gah! Just as Aneurin Donald was beginning to put on another show the heavens open in Brisbane and on come the covers. We don’t currently have enough overs in the bank to call it a game either, that requires five overs of England’s response and they’ve only had 3.5 so far.
Dang and blast. Hopefully the wet stuff moves through and we can at least get an official result. Donald has 31 off 11 balls, he’d just blitzed three consecutive fours off Stanlake.

3rd over: England 32-1 (Donald 18, Brook 8) What a shot from Harry Brook! He digs out a full ball from Meredith and somehow it soars flat like an exocet over cover for SIX! He does it all time time and every time it leaves the jaw on the floor. Remarkable.
“On no!” cries Salt as he is beaten for pace by Stanlake and plinks an easy catch into the off side. England lose their first and it brings captain Harry Brook to the middle. Do not adjust your set.

2nd over: England 22-0 (Salt 3, Donald 18) Donald crouches in his stance and keeps his eyes trained on the ball, leaning into a drive that somehow soars over midwicket for SIX! He didn’t time that at all but the power he has made it not matter a jot. Donald backs away to the next ball and carves over point for four.

1st over: England 9-0 (Salt 1, Donald 8) Salt clips off his pads to get England going. Donald then open his account with flick off his hip fine for four. The Welshman is very much in the shop window for lucrative franchise gigs, India’s wunderkind Vaibhav Sooryavanshi is the only ‘man’ striking the white ball better than him at the moment.
Close! Donald mis-times a pull and it goes high into the leg side but Billy Stanlake slips over haring in to take the catch! That’s a life for Nye.
Here come Salt and Donald. Riley Meredith will start with the ball for Australia, the home side need to make early inroads. Play!
Jamie Overton speaks briefly to the broadcaster after his fantastic 5-12 with the ball. They are the *second-best figures for an Englishman in T20 internationals.
*Go on then – Sam Curran took 5-10 against Afghanistan in the 2022 World Cup. You knew that.
“I hadn’t been bowling well in the first two games, a bit short and a bit erratic. I tried to work on doing the basics well, smashing the top of the stumps.”
Here come England for their response, we might not be here very long BUT YOU NEVER KNOW.
Sam Curran bowls Billy Stanlake and with that subjects Australia to their lowest ever total in T20I cricket.
England have been excellent, razor sharp and clinical. Dare I say it, ruthless .
Bad to worse. Mitch Owen was the man who could have biffed a few boundaries but he has a brain fade and runs himself out attempting a second run that did not exist.
16th over: Australia 108-8 (Owen 16, Meredith 0) Australia are in the mire, Riley Meredith plays out a wicket maiden from Liam Dawson.

Liam Dawson comes back into the attack and Adam Zampa struggles to lay a bat on him… surviving a tight lbw call on review but his slightly tortured innings comes to a close with a nick behind two balls later. Jordan Cox taking a sharp catch behind the sticks.

14th over: Australia 94-7 (Owen 5, Zampa 1) Overton finished with a wicket-maiden and winds up with a brilliant 5-12 from his four overs. He’s single-handedly set England up for victory at the Gabba. Adam Zampa is at the crease for Australia as his fellow spinner Adil Rashid finishes his spell with 0-17. Miserly.

Can Overton pick up a lesser spotted T20I five fer? The Aussies look like they are trying to see him off, Ben Dwarshius is the new batter and he plays out three dots. One ball to come from Overton… there it is! Dwarshius drives and nicks behind! Scenes at the Gabba as Jamie Overton becomes only the second English player to bag a T20I five-fer!

Jamie Overton is playing a blinder! The big man is smashed on the hand off his first ball as he fails to cling onto rasping return catch but he shrugs it off to see the end of Chaudhary with his next ball! Caught a long on, Australia imploding.

12th over: Australia 92-5 (Chaudhary 19, Owen 4) England squeeeeze at the Gabba, Rashid whistles through his third and it only costs two runs. Overton is indeed going to bowl through, here he comes for his fourth.

11th over: Australia 90-5 (Chaudhary 18, Owen 3) Spencer Johnson Mitch Owen comes in for Australia, England sense blood in the water. Jamie Overton has 3-12 from his three overs. He might bowl straight through here too.
Guess who!? Jamie Overton has been involved in all of the dismissals today and he gets the third to his name after bouncing out Joel Davies!

10th over: Australia 86-4 (Chaudhary 17, Davies 3) Rashid again, Chaudhary stays in his own bubble with wickets falling around him, a tidy reverse bring him four. Three singles makes it seven off the over, that’s the halfway stage and England will be very happy with how they are placed. Australia have a longer tail today after choosing to go in with an extra bowler, they might come to regret that decision.

9th over: Australia 79-4 (Chaudhary 11, Davies 2) Joel Davies joins Chaudhary and Australia need to rebuild. Drop! The new man is nearly on his way first ball but Rashid can’t take the diving effort at backward point. Has to go down as a drop but it was a tough one. Still, England on top at the Gabba.

Gone! David tries to pull Overton but doesn’t get enough of it, Henry Crocombe clinging on in the deep. David has a glance at the pitch as he departs but there are no demons there, he was done by cross seam delivery from Overton.
8th over: Australia 71-3 (Chaudhary 11, David 6) Adil Rashid into the attack and he whizzes through a cheap over for England, just six runs off it.

7th over: Australia 71-3 (Chaudhary 6, David 5) Tim David strides to the middle. We all know what he is capable of but England will be buoyed by the three wickets that keep Australia in check. Ouch! Chaudhary is clanged on the helmet by a short one and there’s a brief delay while he is checked over. He’s good to continue and watches David pull the final ball of the over for four.

You can’t keep Jamie Overton out of the action! Brook brings the big fella into the attack and he strikes with a cross seam delivery that JFM tries to launch down the ground… only to find the safe hands of Tom Banton.

6th over: Australia 64-2 (Fraser-McGurk 22, Chaudhary 5) Nikil Chaudhary joins JFM in the middle at the Gabba. He has a look at Dawson for a couple of balls and then sweeps with confidence for four. A clip of the toes brings Fraser-McGurk on strike and he ends the over with a flick for four over wide mid on. Decent contest this, honours around even at the end of the powerplay.
England needed that. Harper plinks a top edge to bucket hands Overton at mid on.

Jake Fraser-McGurk hasn’t had many ball so far and he makes up for it by clubbing two remarkable sixes off the over! A flat batted pull flies over mid on and is followed by an astounding sort of flicked pull over the leg side. Welcome to the party.

A top edge from Harper is meaty enough to fly for SIX over the keeper’s head but it’s a decent over from Crocombe who responds with pace and bounce, beating the bat a couple of times. Nine off the over.

Coles drags down and Harper slams four through the leg side. Pressure on the young Coles here… SIX! Harper backs away to give himself room to blast another big one down the ground. Australia hit back.
2nd over: Australia 14-1 (Fraser-McGurk 2, Harper 1) Sam Harper arrives in the middle, he can hit a long ball. Dawson rattles through his over and England will be very happy with their start.

Spin from both ends to start at the Gabba. Liam Dawson has the second over and removes Marsh with his second ball! Marsh tried to smear into the leg side but an under edge saw the ball plink to Overton at midwicket, the big man swooping to take a good low catch. Early breakthrough for England.

articles.title: North Melbourne defeat Melbourne to win third straight Premiership: 2026 AFLW grand final – as it happened
articles.summary: This blog is now closed Tuning in from around the world and want to know what time first bounce is in your neck of the woods? Don’t look my way, because the AFL has already done the for me! For the fourth straight season – but the first time on a Friday night – the AFLW Grand Final has sold out, with the AFL announcing yesterday that more than 12,500 fans will pack out Princes Park for tonight’s fixture. Continue reading...
articles.content:
North Melbourne entered Friday evening’s AFLW Grand Final at Princes Park in search of history, fighting for the honour of forever being known as the first team in the competition’s history to go back-to-back-to-back as Premiers. They were tasked with overcoming a dogged and determined Melbourne Demons to do so, in sodden conditions in front of a sold-out crowd.

And as champion teams are wont to do, as this team of champions does, they rose to the challenge: absorbing waves of Melbourne pressure before kicking away late to claim the 2026 AFLW Premiership by 26 points, kicking 6.8.44 to Melbourne’s 2.6.18.

Kicking the first three goals of the game, it did appear at one point that the favourites were going to turn this decider into something of a non-event, with it taking until midway through the second half for the Demons to grab their first major.

But that goal from Tayla Harris inspired a revival in the Dees, who raised their physicality, intensity, and determination not just to the level one needs in Grand Finals, in the wet, but the kind of level one needs to reach if you’re to take something from this North side. Tahlia Gillard in defence was immense, serving as the foundation that her side’s effort was built upon and repulsing countless moves forward that would have broken other sides.

With just minutes remaining in the final quarter, the margin was reduced to six points and a grandstand finish beckoned. But the Demons had only been able to snatch points when they needed goals and, when Vikki Wall single-handedly shifted territory into their defensive 50, North struck. First, Bella Eddey snapped a crucial late goal just out of reach of a despairing Gillard to break the back of the Dees’ push, and then Blaithin Bogue added two late majors to cushion the margin.

We’ll have more analysis for you to sink your teeth into tomorrow but, for now, that’s probably a good note to leave on. So that’s what I’ll do – congratulations to North Melbourne: Premiers of the AFLW for 2026 and the first side in competition history to three-peat.

2024 Premiership winner Sarah Wright takes to the stage to present the trophy to Darren Crocker, Jasmine Garner, and Emma Kearney – three recipients for a side that has made history this evening as the first team in AFLW to go back-to-back-to-back.

North coach Darren Crocker congratulates both Melbourne and the rest of the AFLW , noting their investment and what he says is a closing gap at the top.

To the girls… wow! I just just love being your coach. I love coming into work every day, and I’m just so so proud of of what we’ve achieved together.

It’s been two years Down Under for Blaithin Bogue, with two flags to go with it. Not a bad rate of return for the County Fermanagh native, as she reflected to Network Seven.

It’s crazy to be honest. When I decided to come out to Australia, I just wanted to give the sport a crack. Never thought that I’d be a two-time Premiership player. Obviously, very lucky that I got drafted to a great side and great team with great coaches. Very grateful to be here, and yeah, it’s nice to get another Premiership.

When I first came over to Australia. The first year was quite tough. You miss your family, second year, I was sort of getting into the swing of things, and, honestly, I’ve just loved this year. It’s been the most enjoyable year out here.

Kayo Sports grabbed North veteran Emma Kearney after the game, who came up with a pretty apt descriptor of the contest.

That was epic. The Dees had all the momentum and we just had hang on, scrap and we just found a way. To come out on top like that at the end, it was pretty convincing in the end but the scoreboard doesn’t reflect the game.

The best on ground award, no surprise, really, goes to Jasmine Garner.

“To the girls, I’m a bit speechless but I’m so proud: back-to-back-to-back.” she says after receiving the medal.

Jasmine Garner is speaking on the Network Seven coverage and, never mind the threepeat, it seems she’s still getting over how fun playing in that game was.

It’s unbelievable. Everyone’s just just proud. Melbourne were coming and coming in that last quarter. And credit to them; what a bloody great game of footy! For us to kick one, Bella kicks that clutch goal, and when it rains, it pours. And then we got it going from there.

Thanks to her two late strikes, Blaithin Bogue ended the game as its leading goal scorer with two, while, perhaps as expected Ash Riddell and Jasmine Garner were enormous for North with an equal match-leading 26 disposals each. The latter also had three centre clearances, while the former added two of her own.

Tyla Hanks lead the Dees in possessions with 22, to go with two behinds, while Tayla Harris lead all players with six marks – at one stage looking like she was liable to take over even if the conditions and scrappiness of the game was working against her.

It ended in disappointment, but Gillard was enormous for the Demons down back, too, coming up with 15 intercepts, with teammate Sinead Goldrick and her ten the only other player in double digits.

North Melbourne are the first club in AFLW history to win three straight premierships.

Melbourne threw themselves forward with every ounce of vile and venom in their veins as they tried to pull off an improbable upset but in one dramatic moment, Wall’s decisive intercept and clearance to completely flip territory turned the game on its head.

From there, the AFLW’s premiere dynasty were able to go to work, getting a huge goal through Eddey to drive a stake through Melbourne’s hopes, and Bogue then delivering the coup de grâce with two late goals.

North takes the 2026 AFLW decider by 26 points, kicking 6.8.44 to Melbourne’s 2.6.18.

Bogue runs onto a loose ball atop the Dees goal square and soccers it home; the Kangas are going to threepeat in style.

After a rushed behind, Ash Riddell looks like she’s going to go the torp for a sealer and while she can’t make the distance in the wet, it falls into the waiting hands of Bogue.

She snatches the ball from 35 out and snaps it forward and despite the desperate attempts to retreat and clear it away by Gillard, it makes its way through for a major!

The margin is now 13 points with two minutes remaining – surely a match winning margin for a North defence like this.

What a moment. North have been under siege for pretty much the entire last quarter but Vikki Wall has charged down Heath-Barker and just hoofed the ball into empty space forward, completely shifting the territory battle.

Afforded some breathing space, North then grabs a point through Bruton and pushes the margin back out to seven.

Pearce grabs the ball out of the ruck from a throw-in and is just able to get it to Hanks, but her snap shot goes just wide!

But Melbourne has continued to chip away, meaning the margin is down to a straight kick.

The Demons want a free kick against Kearney for holding the ball but it’s going to be a ball-up instead. And then another.

Hanks roves a kick intended for Harris and swings another shot towards goal but this one bounces wide for a throw-in. Harris, uncontested, punches the ball forward and it bounces through for a point.

The Dees have their first points since the final seconds of the second quarter but it’s just a solitary one, as Hanks drags an effort low and across the face of goal.

This game is turning into almost a pitched battle; the buffeting rain and intensity giving the contest a brutal edge.

The Dees have lift their intensity as they look to lock the ball in their attacking 50 but every time they look for an opening, it’s immediately closed down by a swarm of North players – Ferguson making multiple interventions to maintain her side’s nine point lead.

Bruton refuses to be denied and, on the third time of asking, wins a free kick out on the left wing. But Gillard is there once more when the ball eventually makes it way closer to the Dees goal, repulsing the danger and springing them forward.

Kylie Minogue rings out as the crowd rises in anticipation of the bounce marking the commencement of the final quarter of the 2026 AFLW Grand Final.

The desperation, fatigue, pressure, and weather came to the fore in the Premiership quarter, with neither side able to convert a six pointer and the Dees held off the scoreboard entirely.

Gillard continues to stand up and be counted but, as we’ve almost come to take for granted over the past few years, North’s structure has proven superb in locking down their defensive 50 – and they’ve to a nine point lead to defend heading into the final term.

Paxman makes another series of important interventions at the last to keep North at bay. Kate Shierlaw is able to send a snap shot on goal from a ball up for the Kangas but it goes wide.

The combination of the wet weather and the sheer desperation of finals footy means that players have nary a moment to breath in possession before they’re being enveloped by pressure from their opponents.

Chaplin sends an effort towards goal but Amy Mangan gets back on the last line to intercept. North marches up the other end but another huge effort from Fitzsimon wins a holding the ball and springs the Dees forward in attack.

A holding the ball call gives Bogue a chance to boot North’s fourth but she sends her attempt wide, the lead extending to eight rather 13.

Chaplin is taken high and booms her free kick from the top of the 50 long. Harris flies but can’t grab it and Emma Kearney pokes it clear.

Garner finds the ball in the middle of the park and boots the ball forward. And while Sarah Lampard has time to retreat to the top of the goal square, her clearance goes straight to Jenna Bruton, only for the North forward to hang her kick up at the top of the goal square.

Another big smother, this time from Tyla Hanks, frustrates North’s efforts to grab a major within seconds for a third-straight quarter.

Randall gets a good look moments later for another attempt but she pulls her effort wide for a point.

Led by Garner’s 13 disposals and goal, North led by 19 points at one point in that second quarter and could have easily kicked away with it – we’ve seen hints that they’re very much capable of that at times this evening.

But with Harris taking a few huge grabs – including one to set up her side’s first goal – the Dees have been able to lock things down and slowly work their way back into the contest.

Gillard has been vital in their efforts, here, with the defender leading all players on the park with seven intercept possessions, while Goldrick and Maeve Chaplin have four apiece. And that smother from Paxman to deny Garner certainly stopped a North goal.

With rain coming down increasingly heavy at Princes Park, it’s anybody’s game heading into this second-half; just the way we like it.

After being down two goals at the first break and then a third within seconds of the second quarter opening, efforts from Harris and Fitzsimon ensure that the Dees will head into halftime down just a the single major.

The Dees get their second with just moments remaining in the second quarter through Fitzsimon!

paragraphs: North Melbourne entered Friday evening’s AFLW Grand Final at Princes Park in search of history, fighting for the honour of forever being known as the first team in the competition’s history to go back-to-back-to-back as Premiers. They were tasked with overcoming a dogged and determined Melbourne Demons to do so, in sodden conditions in front of a sold-out crowd.

And as champion teams are wont to do, as this team of champions does, they rose to the challenge: absorbing waves of Melbourne pressure before kicking away late to claim the 2026 AFLW Premiership by 26 points, kicking 6.8.44 to Melbourne’s 2.6.18.

Kicking the first three goals of the game, it did appear at one point that the favourites were going to turn this decider into something of a non-event, with it taking until midway through the second half for the Demons to grab their first major.

But that goal from Tayla Harris inspired a revival in the Dees, who raised their physicality, intensity, and determination not just to the level one needs in Grand Finals, in the wet, but the kind of level one needs to reach if you’re to take something from this North side. Tahlia Gillard in defence was immense, serving as the foundation that her side’s effort was built upon and repulsing countless moves forward that would have broken other sides.

With just minutes remaining in the final quarter, the margin was reduced to six points and a grandstand finish beckoned. But the Demons had only been able to snatch points when they needed goals and, when Vikki Wall single-handedly shifted territory into their defensive 50, North struck. First, Bella Eddey snapped a crucial late goal just out of reach of a despairing Gillard to break the back of the Dees’ push, and then Blaithin Bogue added two late majors to cushion the margin.

We’ll have more analysis for you to sink your teeth into tomorrow but, for now, that’s probably a good note to leave on. So that’s what I’ll do – congratulations to North Melbourne: Premiers of the AFLW for 2026 and the first side in competition history to three-peat.

2024 Premiership winner Sarah Wright takes to the stage to present the trophy to Darren Crocker, Jasmine Garner, and Emma Kearney – three recipients for a side that has made history this evening as the first team in AFLW to go back-to-back-to-back.
North coach Darren Crocker congratulates both Melbourne and the rest of the AFLW , noting their investment and what he says is a closing gap at the top.
To the girls… wow! I just just love being your coach. I love coming into work every day, and I’m just so so proud of of what we’ve achieved together.
It’s been two years Down Under for Blaithin Bogue, with two flags to go with it. Not a bad rate of return for the County Fermanagh native, as she reflected to Network Seven.

It’s crazy to be honest. When I decided to come out to Australia, I just wanted to give the sport a crack. Never thought that I’d be a two-time Premiership player. Obviously, very lucky that I got drafted to a great side and great team with great coaches. Very grateful to be here, and yeah, it’s nice to get another Premiership.

When I first came over to Australia. The first year was quite tough. You miss your family, second year, I was sort of getting into the swing of things, and, honestly, I’ve just loved this year. It’s been the most enjoyable year out here.
Kayo Sports grabbed North veteran Emma Kearney after the game, who came up with a pretty apt descriptor of the contest.

That was epic. The Dees had all the momentum and we just had hang on, scrap and we just found a way. To come out on top like that at the end, it was pretty convincing in the end but the scoreboard doesn’t reflect the game.
The best on ground award, no surprise, really, goes to Jasmine Garner.
“To the girls, I’m a bit speechless but I’m so proud: back-to-back-to-back.” she says after receiving the medal.
Jasmine Garner is speaking on the Network Seven coverage and, never mind the threepeat, it seems she’s still getting over how fun playing in that game was.

It’s unbelievable. Everyone’s just just proud. Melbourne were coming and coming in that last quarter. And credit to them; what a bloody great game of footy! For us to kick one, Bella kicks that clutch goal, and when it rains, it pours. And then we got it going from there.

Thanks to her two late strikes, Blaithin Bogue ended the game as its leading goal scorer with two, while, perhaps as expected Ash Riddell and Jasmine Garner were enormous for North with an equal match-leading 26 disposals each. The latter also had three centre clearances, while the former added two of her own.

Tyla Hanks lead the Dees in possessions with 22, to go with two behinds, while Tayla Harris lead all players with six marks – at one stage looking like she was liable to take over even if the conditions and scrappiness of the game was working against her.
It ended in disappointment, but Gillard was enormous for the Demons down back, too, coming up with 15 intercepts, with teammate Sinead Goldrick and her ten the only other player in double digits.
North Melbourne are the first club in AFLW history to win three straight premierships.

Melbourne threw themselves forward with every ounce of vile and venom in their veins as they tried to pull off an improbable upset but in one dramatic moment, Wall’s decisive intercept and clearance to completely flip territory turned the game on its head.

From there, the AFLW’s premiere dynasty were able to go to work, getting a huge goal through Eddey to drive a stake through Melbourne’s hopes, and Bogue then delivering the coup de grâce with two late goals.
North takes the 2026 AFLW decider by 26 points, kicking 6.8.44 to Melbourne’s 2.6.18.
Bogue runs onto a loose ball atop the Dees goal square and soccers it home; the Kangas are going to threepeat in style.
After a rushed behind, Ash Riddell looks like she’s going to go the torp for a sealer and while she can’t make the distance in the wet, it falls into the waiting hands of Bogue.
She snatches the ball from 35 out and snaps it forward and despite the desperate attempts to retreat and clear it away by Gillard, it makes its way through for a major!
The margin is now 13 points with two minutes remaining – surely a match winning margin for a North defence like this.

What a moment. North have been under siege for pretty much the entire last quarter but Vikki Wall has charged down Heath-Barker and just hoofed the ball into empty space forward, completely shifting the territory battle.
Afforded some breathing space, North then grabs a point through Bruton and pushes the margin back out to seven.

articles.content:
The so-bad-it’s-good holiday film has become a new festive tradition. Stars Maddie Ziegler and Dennis Quaid explain why they’re so hard to resist

“W ith the state of the world right now, people want an escape,” says Maddie Ziegler. The 24-year-old performer first shot to fame on the Lifetime reality show Dance Moms in 2011, before becoming the unlikely muse of the publicity-shy singer Sia , which led to a role in Steven Spielberg ’s West Side Story. Ziegler’s latest project is In a Holidaze , a fuzzy Christmas movie that comes to Netflix on 2 December. “I’ve actually never done a romcom before,” she says, speaking on a recent Zoom call from Los Angeles. “I grew up loving Christmas movies so much, so when this came into my lap, I was so excited.’”

In the film, Ziegler plays Maelyn – a restless twentysomething who finds herself trapped in a holiday time-loop, where she’s forced to relive the same Christmas at her family’s picturesque cabin until she learns to trust her gut and take chances on what makes her happy. This sugary-sweet movie might be new territory for Ziegler, but it’s exactly the type of film we’ve come to expect from Netflix. The streamer’s Christmas originals usually revolve around romance and family, with an aesthetic quality and winking irony that feels similar to Hallmark – the American card-maker turned movie giant, whose very name is synonymous with cliches.

Netflix’s festive movies often feel like they purposefully riff off existing films. Common motifs include unlikely romances, time-travel, body-switching, fictional royalty from non-existent countries, and all kinds of low-stakes situations that, of course, must be fixed in time for Christmas. During a conversation with In a Holidaze writer and director Tiffany Paulsen, I described the film as “ Groundhog Day meets The Family Stone ”. Paulsen was thrilled to be in the company of such “amazing, iconic references”, noting that the core of every Christmas movie comes back to family. “The holiday tradition is people coming together, whether that’s your traditional family or your chosen family,” she says. “That’s the universal element in all of these stories.”

These films also tap into nostalgia. Even the mere mention of 90s heartthrob Quaid makes millennials like me long for the days of watching the 1998 classic The Parent Trap on VHS tape. Quaid, who stars in A Dog’s Perfect Christmas, tells me that new festive films tap into a “yearning” for a time before smartphones. “The 90s was about family,” he says, “and it was the last decade of analogue.” He even jokes about how, in today’s hyper-connected world, the twins in The Parent Trap would have been easily rumbled. “Those kids would have been tracked on their phones by parental controls,” Quaid laughs. “They would have been like, ‘What’s this international bill I’m getting on my account?!’”

The Parent Trap made Lindsay Lohan a generational star, so it’s no surprise that she has also appeared in a handful of Netflix’s festive films. In fact, it’s become a pattern for these movies to be a vehicle for actors who first made their name in TV shows or films from the 2000s to reconnect with their (now slightly older) audience. This year, Padalecki and Milo Ventimiglia – who fans first met as romantic rivals in Gilmore Girls – both appear in separate Netflix Christmas films. Padalecki tells me that the rise of streaming platforms, plus the ability to watch TV virtually anywhere on any device, has given the show – and by extension, him – a whole new level of cultural relevance. “When I was on Gilmore Girls , in 2000-2005, it wasn’t yet the show it is now,” he says. “It was big, but it wasn’t like everybody has seen it and re-watches it every fall.”

In fact, Padalecki thinks Netflix might have tapped him for this project because the millennial ritual of rewatching the show makes him feel innately familiar to people. “With TV, you’re in their home, you’re playing in the background when they’re cooking dinner, or they’re taking out the garbage, or helping their kids with homework,” he says. “And as they’re doing that, they’re hearing your voice.”

The answer might be that Netflix’s cheap and cheerful Christmas movies are surprisingly popular. A representative for Netflix UK tells me that, every week in December 2025, there were six or more holiday movies in the UK’s weekly top 10, which rose to seven in 10 in the final two weeks of the year. On the day I spoke to Quaid, A Dog’s Perfect Christmas had just become Netflix’s top movie globally – despite a response from reviewers I will charitably describe as lukewarm . And as Americans prepare to travel home for Thanksgiving, Guarding Stars also hit the global top spot.

The conundrum for Netflix is whether its undeniably impressive metrics translate into content that is genuinely loved by audiences. But even so, its Hallmark-coded Christmas films feel like an exception to the rule, because it seems like a sense of disassociation is actually the point. “Holiday movies are sort of like a safety net where everything’s going to be OK,” says Christina Hobbs, one half of Christina Lauren, the duo who co-wrote the 2020 novel that In a Holidaze is based on. “I just think people really need that right now.” Lauren Billings, her co-writer, agrees that these stories often soothe the anxieties of younger viewers in particular. “There’s not enough jobs, young people think they’re never going to make it, or they’re never going to be able to buy a house,” she says. “And so I think that we crave that sense of comfort and reassurance.”

Films like A Dog’s Perfect Christmas might not be winning the Palme d’Or at Cannes any time soon, but considering that there is a long tradition of Christmas-themed art purposefully playing with our ideas of “high” and “low” brow, it’s difficult to take umbrage with films that allow people to briefly escape into a world of cliches and candy canes. “I feel like what we do is so important,” says Paulsen. “We give people a moment of love and warmth and laughter, as cheesy as it sounds.”

In a Holidaze is out on Netflix on 2 December; A Dog’s Perfect Christmas and Guardian Stars are out now

articles.title: ‘I was very aggressive. They threw me out of every school’ … Julie Delpy on acting, anger and predatory directors
articles.summary: Thirty years after the roles that made her famous, the star of Three Colours: White and the Before trilogy is busier than ever – as a screenwriter and director. But, she says, a lot of people have tried to keep her down To listen to Julie Delpy talk about her workload is to feel the need for a nap coming on. She is writing six screenplays at the moment that range from dark comedies to thrillers. “I don’t do monoculture,” she says. If her producer hadn’t reined her in, she would be working on five horror film scripts too. The actor, writer and director says she doesn’t sleep well – she can sit at her desk for up to 18 hours, writing “until I run out of steam. I know you could think I’m exaggerating. I’m not. If you look at my computer, you will see how bad it is.” We’re on a video call, Delpy from her home in Los Angeles. She is charming – intense and funny in big black-framed glasses. “I look so weird with this angle on my hair,” she says, of the ceiling light behind her. “Like an angry bald man!” Continue reading...

At 13, at an audition, she says she was alone with a director in his apartment when he asked her to take her clothes off. “I took the script and threw it in his face,” says Delpy. She told her parents. “I said: ‘I don’t want to be an actress if that’s what it means.’ And they were like: ‘Well, look at us. We didn’t do that.’”

Other early experiences were better. Delpy’s first film role was in Jean-Luc Godard’s Detective. “It was great to work with him, and he was such a nice guy,” she says. “I mean, he was not a nice guy” – the influential French director was notoriously volatile and difficult – “but with me he was incredibly nice and respectful, and protective.”

But sexual harassment as a young woman in Hollywood was unavoidable. “I remember this guy, who’s still around, a very powerful guy. He tried to break into the bathroom where I was at a party.” She has spoken before about turning down a director’s sexual advances around the same time, when she was in her early 20s, and that he had spread word in the business that she was “difficult”. “The minute you say no to people …” She pauses. “And also the way I was expressing myself, I was very straightforward.”

When Harvey Weinstein’s company Miramax was involved in releasing the second part of the Three Colours trilogy, White, in which Delpy starred, she says she chose to stay in a different hotel from him because of the rumours she had heard. “I was not naive because I was coming from France, where it was like, you were dodging the paedophiles basically,” she says with a grim laugh. “I had the luck to not be a young girl from the midwest who has no idea what’s going on.”

Making Before Sunrise (1995), in which she plays Céline, a beautiful young free spirit who spends a night in Vienna with Jesse (Ethan Hawke), Delpy says she contributed many lines and ideas to the script and was frustrated that this wasn’t recognised with a writing credit. “I went through a really rough time in my late 20s but it took me reading my journal to actually know that. I was like: ‘Oh, that sounds like a breakdown.’” On the surface, she says, most people wouldn’t have known anything was wrong. “I wouldn’t cry and stay alone.” Instead, she felt a lot of anger. “I was doing quite a lot of drinking.”

She was, however, along with Hawke, recognised as a writer on the sequel, Before Sunset , which was nominated for a best adapted screenplay Oscar. When Before Sunrise was released, she says, it wasn’t a big success. “It grew with the second film. Even when I was writing the second one, my agent fired me, saying I was wasting my time writing a sequel to a little indie film that no one gave a shit about, and I should be going on auditions instead of writing.”

Delpy doesn’t come across as bitter, but she is evidently still angry. “People have hurt me in this business,” she says. When I ask her to elaborate, she talks vaguely, mentioning people “telling me I was stupid. Trying to break my confidence.” Just a few years ago, she says, a financier pulled out of her sci-fi drama My Zoe at the last minute, put off, she believes, by someone briefing against her. “There’s still a system that’s trying to keep people where they want them to be,” she says.

Delpy always wanted to write and direct, and she made her first film, Blah Blah Blah, a short that was shown at Sundance, in 1995. She never wanted to be typecast as the ingenue. “I was able to get out of that pretty quickly,” she says. It became even more important to create her own work as she got older in an industry where good parts for middle-aged actors are still scarce. Twenty years ago, it was even worse. “Yeah, I didn’t love some of the stuff, so I started writing.” She created and starred in the 2021 Netflix series On the Verge, about the lives of four women in their late 40s, but it lasted for only one season. “I don’t know what happened,” she says, but “the algorithm doesn’t love women in that age group apparently”.

Next year Delpy is in a Ruben Östlund comedy with Keanu Reeves, The Entertainment System Is Down, and in actor Sonoya Mizuno’s directorial debut, Stages, about a young dancer at an elite ballet school. She is regularly asked about a fourth Before film but says 2013’s Before Midnight is the last one. “Richard approached us at one point, but the idea didn’t really go very far.” Reportedly, her character, Céline, was going to die. “I wasn’t into it. Ethan was not really into it, and Richard was not really into it. Nobody liked it.” She laughs. “Now we’ve passed the time that we were supposed to do it. It’s a trilogy. We’ll never know what happens to them.”

Does she feel – as I do when I watch those films – sad and wistful for the feeling of time passing, and what might have been? No, says Delpy, “I’m really excited about the future.” She says it was good to revisit the journals of her childhood and youth, “but now I’ve done it, I’m focusing on stuff I’m writing”. Those six (and counting) screenplays are calling and she’s energised because she thinks they are among her best work. It’s all she can do not to become completely consumed by them.

She says she has to make an effort to see people, “because I’m so happy in my world. You create a world and you live in it. I know it’s a film, but it’s also like jumping into a parallel universe. It’s the most fun thing in the world. I love making films because what was only in your head becomes something tangible.” She pauses. “I’m not saying all of this is great. A lot of it might end up turning shit, right? But, you know, I’m doing it anyway.”

articles.content:
Musician who had huge 1980s chart success had been diagnosed with prostate cancer in 2018

Duran Duran was transformed by Andy Taylor’s rock edge – and never quite the same without him

Andy Taylor, the guitarist with 80s pop megastars Duran Duran , has died aged 65.

He had been diagnosed with stage four metastatic prostate cancer in 2018, which he disclosed publicly in 2022 when Duran Duran were about to be inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame.

“To the world, Andy was a brilliant guitarist, but to us, he was the most wonderful husband, a loving dad and the proudest grandfather,” read a statement shared with Variety . “He was the rock of our family. For all the incredible experiences music brought him, family always came first. Nothing made him happier than having us all together, and no matter how far music took him, his heart was always at home.”

Taylor’s wife of more than 40 years, Tracey Wilson said his last few years were faced with “so much courage and determination” and that he “never los[t] his love of life”.

A statement from Duran Duran added: “Andy was there at the very beginning of our story. From the moment he arrived in Birmingham from the North East with a guitar and an unshakeable belief in what we could become, he brought an indelible fire and swagger to our music. His playing drove the songs that took us around the world, and with a dry wit that was matched only by his wonderfully unsentimental, no-nonsense outlook on life he kept us grounded and gave the band its edge through the extraordinary years that followed.”

Musicians paid tribute once the news broke. Rod Stewart remembered Taylor as his “dear pal”.

“We made some good music together and at the same time had some outrageous fun,” Stewart wrote on Instagram.

Singer Belinda Carlisle called Taylor a “genius”. “He played the guitar solo on Mad About You, appears in the video and he made special appearances onstage for some of my first solo shows. What a talent,” she captioned a video of the pair performing together.

“Thank you Andy for the music and all of the joy you brought to the world which will live on forever. I hope you are feeling the love… Godspeed.”

Taylor was born in 1961 and grew up in Cullercoats, Northumberland, in a family who worked in the local fishing industry. He began playing guitar from the age of 11 and was tutored by Dave Black of the David Bowie backing band the Spiders from Mars. He left school early to start playing in bands on the working men’s club scene.

In 1980 he joined the nascent Duran Duran, who had formed in 1978 but whose lineup was far from settled – they advertised for a guitarist in Melody Maker, and Taylor travelled to Birmingham to audition. “A couple of days later they rang me and said out of 40 or so I was the only one who knew how to tune up, let alone play,” he later recalled.

The following month Simon Le Bon joined as frontman, by February 1981 they had released their debut single Planet Earth, and with the July release of Girls on Film – a song propelled by Taylor’s ultra-tight and rhythmic playing – they became major stars in the UK and US. Rio, their second album released in 1982, cemented their international playboy image and went Top 10 in both countries, and follow-up Seven and the Ragged Tiger topped the UK chart. Speaking to Smash Hits in 1983, Taylor described his new-found career as “a hobby gone mad”. That year Taylor also opened a wine bar called Rio, in Whitley Bay in his native Tyneside.

Following their third album Duran Duran went on a brief hiatus, during which time Taylor and bassist John Taylor (no relation) formed a new funk-rock group, the Power Station, with singer Robert Palmer and former Chic drummer Tony Thompson. Two singles, the original track Some Like It Hot and a cover of T Rex’s Get It On, reached the US Top 10 in 1985.

Later that year Taylor rejoined Duran Duran to record A View to a Kill, the US chart-topping James Bond film theme, and perform with them at Live Aid in Philadelphia. But amid drug use, relations had become strained: drummer Roger Taylor left due to exhaustion, and Andy Taylor himself left to pursue the rockier direction he began with the Power Station – though his Duran Duran bandmates initially believed he would be continuing with the band.

“I’d come close to a nervous breakdown from the stresses of our crazy life and my own cocaine problem,” Taylor later said. “Combine that with all the shouting matches and the icy silences – I just knew I had to get out. So I did. The day after Live Aid, I stopped drinking and taking drugs. And I quietly started getting legal advice on extricating myself from Duran Duran.”

Collaborating with Sex Pistols’ Steve Jones, he released a solo LP, Thunder, in 1986, and the single Take It Easy was a minor US hit. As well as recording a covers album, Dangerous, he spent a number of years as a writer and producer for hire, with his song Lost in You becoming a transatlantic hit for Rod Stewart in 1988.

The Power Station briefly reunited in 1996, and then in 2000, the classic lineup of Duran Duran reformed and released a new album together, Astronaut, in 2004. He also toured with the band and worked on another (later scrapped) album Reportage, but was hit hard by the death of his father to cancer, and left the band again in 2006; he was diagnosed with depression the following year.

He spent the next decade away from music, first publishing his memoir Wild Boy: My Life in Duran Duran in 2008. He released a new solo single in 2019 and joined British rock band Reef as a tour guitarist, also producing their 2022 album Shoot Me Your Ace.

Despite the at-times fractious relationship with Duran Duran over the years, Taylor said in his statement accompanying the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame induction that there was no “bad blood … just pure love and respect for everything we wrote, recorded and achieved together”.

He married Wilson in 1982, and they had four children together: Andrew, Georgina, Bethany and Isabella.

Following his cancer diagnosis, he credited his successful music career with keeping him upbeat. “I’ve been very fortunate, I’ve had so much, in terms of living the dream, but because I do music, I think that’s probably really helped me to live with pessimism of an incurable disease,” he said.

“I’d come close to a nervous breakdown from the stresses of our crazy life and my own cocaine problem,” Taylor later said. “Combine that with all the shouting matches and the icy silences – I just knew I had to get out. So I did. The day after Live Aid, I stopped drinking and taking drugs. And I quietly started getting legal advice on extricating myself from Duran Duran.”

Collaborating with Sex Pistols’ Steve Jones, he released a solo LP, Thunder, in 1986, and the single Take It Easy was a minor US hit. As well as recording a covers album, Dangerous, he spent a number of years as a writer and producer for hire, with his song Lost in You becoming a transatlantic hit for Rod Stewart in 1988.

The Power Station briefly reunited in 1996, and then in 2000, the classic lineup of Duran Duran reformed and released a new album together, Astronaut, in 2004. He also toured with the band and worked on another (later scrapped) album Reportage, but was hit hard by the death of his father to cancer, and left the band again in 2006; he was diagnosed with depression the following year.

He spent the next decade away from music, first publishing his memoir Wild Boy: My Life in Duran Duran in 2008. He released a new solo single in 2019 and joined British rock band Reef as a tour guitarist, also producing their 2022 album Shoot Me Your Ace.

Despite the at-times fractious relationship with Duran Duran over the years, Taylor said in his statement accompanying the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame induction that there was no “bad blood … just pure love and respect for everything we wrote, recorded and achieved together”.
He married Wilson in 1982, and they had four children together: Andrew, Georgina, Bethany and Isabella.

Following his cancer diagnosis, he credited his successful music career with keeping him upbeat. “I’ve been very fortunate, I’ve had so much, in terms of living the dream, but because I do music, I think that’s probably really helped me to live with pessimism of an incurable disease,” he said.

articles.content:
Dario Russo’s debut feature is Brothers Grimm meets Yorgos Lanthimos, with a standout cast including Olivia Colman, Sam Neill and Emily Browning

T he vibe of writer-director Dario Russo’s delightfully peculiar feature debut is “messed-up fairytale”, pitched somewhere between the Brothers Grimm and Yorgos Lanthimos, with a distinctly Australian je ne sais quoi .

Russo is perhaps best known for co-creating the spy comedy series Danger 5, which had an aesthetic inspired by 60s and 70s men’s magazines; The Fox has a similarly thick retro texture. I love how this film feels as though it was made in consultation with the animal world, taking place in a universe where animals can speak to humans – though that’s perhaps the least weird thing about it.

The eponymous fox is voiced by Olivia Colman and the film opens with her reflecting on the true nature and “peculiar interests” of various species. Cats, for instance, are “torturers”, “frogs are sex pests” and “dogs are degenerates”. But human beings, she says, are the strangest of all, because “they like to make themselves miserable” and “pretend they have no say in their own misery”.

The subsequent narrative involves characters whose lives may be miserable but whose behaviour is entertaining. Taking place in a small Australian town, The Fox revolves around two couples: Kori (Emily Browning) and her boyfriend, Nick (Jai Courtney), and Derek (Damon Herriman) and his wife, Diana (Claudia Doumit). Kori and Derek, who are both veterinarians, are having an affair. Nick has no idea, and we see him propose to Kori at the local pub. After a nervous pause, she nods yes – but there’s something a little off, her countenance oddly worried and sad given the circumstances.

When Nick gets wind of the affair, he takes the view that his relationship with Kori is otherwise rock-solid. He is therefore receptive to taking unconventional romantic advice from an unconventional source: Colman’s fox, who assures him that she knows how to “put everything back to normal”. All Nick has to do is push Kori into a large magical hole, his bushy-tailed confidante assures him, and she’ll emerge a perfectly loyal partner.

This hole isn’t a rabbit hole but, in terms of metaphorical implications, it might as well be, connecting one (already warped) reality to another. Nick takes the fox’s advice – it’d be a bland movie if he didn’t – and deals with the increasingly strange fallout, which extends into plot revelations that involve the broader populace. Perhaps he should have listened to the local magpie, who warns him that the fox is “full of shit” and he’s heading for a “world of pain”.

Voiced by the late and great Sam Neill , this feathered harbinger of doom is blessed with a peculiar nasal whine, as though Neill delivered his lines with fingers clamped over his nostrils. His vocal performance is both funny weird and funny ha-ha, suiting the film’s spaced-out spirit. The same goes for Browning, whose portrayal of Kori changes significantly after act one, growing more eccentric as the film gets zanier. Courtney is also in fine form: as the runtime progresses, there’s no ignoring that panicked look in his eyes – the gaze of somebody who knows they have crossed a point of no return.

I won’t disclose where the plot spirals but suffice to say the film’s message is: careful what you wish for. This is delivered with a great deal more flair than in the similarly themed and overrated Obsession , which reduces its female lead to a brainless ghoul while doing little with its intriguing core idea: that loving someone too much can become a nightmare.

Russo is up to something different here; something a bit cheeky and witchy. The film’s narrative and visual flavour (props to its cinematographer, Matthew Chuang, who also shot You Won’t Be Alone and Of an Age ) come together beautifully, as if the entire production has been cooked up in a misty forest by the light of the moon. That’d be a full moon , of course: a beacon for weirdos, peculiar transformations and all manner of kooky shenanigans.

The Fox is in Australian cinemas from Thursday, US cinemas from 4 December and it will get a digital release in the UK and Ireland on 11 January
